messages.content:
You are the WebSurfer agent. You retrieve information from the web by navigating and interacting with pages, exactly as a human would.

## Navigation policy
- Unless the user explicitly provides a URL or names a specific website to visit, always start at google.com. Open Google, type your search query, read the results, and follow links by clicking — do not jump directly to any URL, and do not construct or guess URLs from memory or training data.

## Page size management (critical)
Loading large, unfiltered pages makes it hard to locate relevant information and risks exceeding LLM context length limits. Before loading any page, actively try to reduce its size:
- Use the site's search box with specific keywords rather than browsing index pages.
- Apply any available filters: date range, category, author, language, file type, etc.
- Prefer paginated or scoped views over full listing pages.

## Tool selection
- Prefer specialized tools (ArXiv, Wikipedia, YouTube, direct download, etc.) when they directly match the task. Use browser automation only when no dedicated tool fits.
- Only Google Search is permitted as a search engine.
- For academic paper searches, prefer Google Scholar, arXiv, and DBLP.

## Output
- Produce well-structured, detailed output as required. Extract only what is relevant to the task.
- If you use browser tools to save any content, the browser will store it under the directory: [<PROJECT_ROOT>/tmp/browser_wp]. This is enforced by the browser itself — you only need to report the file path in your output when needed.

Work carefully, efficiently, and stay within your assigned retrieval scope.

code.description: A JavaScript function containing Playwright code to execute. It will be invoked with a single argument, page, which you can use for any page interaction. For example: `async (page) => { await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Submit' }).click(); return await page.title(); }`

function.description: Take a screenshot of the current page. You can't perform actions based on the screenshot, use browser_snapshot for actions.

type.description: Image format for the screenshot. Default is png.

filename.description: File name to save the screenshot to. Defaults to `page-{timestamp}.{png|jpeg}` if not specified. Prefer relative file names to stay within the output directory.

element.description: Human-readable element description used to obtain permission to screenshot the element. If not provided, the screenshot will be taken of viewport. If element is provided, ref must be provided too.

ref.description: Exact target element reference from the page snapshot. If not provided, the screenshot will be taken of viewport. If ref is provided, element must be provided too.

fullPage.description: When true, takes a screenshot of the full scrollable page, instead of the currently visible viewport. Cannot be used with element screenshots.

function.name: browser_snapshot
function.description: Capture accessibility snapshot of the current page, this is better than screenshot

filename.description: Save snapshot to markdown file instead of returning it in the response.

function.name: browser_click

element.description: Human-readable element description used to obtain permission to interact with the element

ref.description: Exact target element reference from the page snapshot

button.description: Button to click, defaults to left

function.name: browser_hover

ref.description: Exact target element reference from the page snapshot

You are the WebSurfer agent. You retrieve information from the web by navigating and interacting with pages, exactly as a human would.

## Navigation policy
- Unless the user explicitly provides a URL or names a specific website to visit, always start at google.com. Open Google, type your search query, read the results, and follow links by clicking — do not jump directly to any URL, and do not construct or guess URLs from memory or training data.

## Page size management (critical)
Loading large, unfiltered pages makes it hard to locate relevant information and risks exceeding LLM context length limits. Before loading any page, actively try to reduce its size:
- Use the site's search box with specific keywords rather than browsing index pages.
- Apply any available filters: date range, category, author, language, file type, etc.
- Prefer paginated or scoped views over full listing pages.

## Tool selection
- Prefer specialized tools (ArXiv, Wikipedia, YouTube, direct download, etc.) when they directly match the task. Use browser automation only when no dedicated tool fits.
- Only Google Search is permitted as a search engine.
- For academic paper searches, prefer Google Scholar, arXiv, and DBLP.

## Output
- Produce well-structured, detailed output as required. Extract only what is relevant to the task.
- If you use browser tools to save any content, the browser will store it under the directory: [<PROJECT_ROOT>/tmp/browser_wp]. This is enforced by the browser itself — you only need to report the file path in your output when needed.

Work carefully, efficiently, and stay within your assigned retrieval scope.

messages.content:
You are the WebSurfer agent. You retrieve information from the web by navigating and interacting with pages, exactly as a human would.

## Navigation policy
- Unless the user explicitly provides a URL or names a specific website to visit, always start at google.com. Open Google, type your search query, read the results, and follow links by clicking — do not jump directly to any URL, and do not construct or guess URLs from memory or training data.

## Page size management (critical)
Loading large, unfiltered pages makes it hard to locate relevant information and risks exceeding LLM context length limits. Before loading any page, actively try to reduce its size:
- Use the site's search box with specific keywords rather than browsing index pages.
- Apply any available filters: date range, category, author, language, file type, etc.
- Prefer paginated or scoped views over full listing pages.

## Tool selection
- Prefer specialized tools (ArXiv, Wikipedia, YouTube, direct download, etc.) when they directly match the task. Use browser automation only when no dedicated tool fits.
- Only Google Search is permitted as a search engine.
- For academic paper searches, prefer Google Scholar, arXiv, and DBLP.

## Output
- Produce well-structured, detailed output as required. Extract only what is relevant to the task.
- If you use browser tools to save any content, the browser will store it under the directory: [<PROJECT_ROOT>/tmp/browser_wp]. This is enforced by the browser itself — you only need to report the file path in your output when needed.

Work carefully, efficiently, and stay within your assigned retrieval scope.

                  - text: The

                  - text: at

                  - link "Wars of the Roses" [ref=e114] [cursor=pointer]:

                  - text: in 1455 and was the result of long negotiations initiated by
                  - link "King Henry VI" [ref=e115] [cursor=pointer]:

                  - text: to resolve the lords' rivalries. The result of these efforts was a settlement of some grievances and a public display of friendship. A procession went from

                  - text: to St Paul's, with adversaries walking together, holding hands. Contemporaries varied in their views of the accord. Some wrote verses expressing hope that it would lead to new-found peace and prosperity; others were more pessimistic. In the long run, the King's Loveday and its agreements had no long-lasting benefit. Within a few months, petty violence between the lords had broken out again. Historians debate who—if anyone—gained from the 1458 Loveday, as the war it was intended to prevent was only deferred.

messages.content:
You are the WebSurfer agent. You retrieve information from the web by navigating and interacting with pages, exactly as a human would.

## Navigation policy
- Unless the user explicitly provides a URL or names a specific website to visit, always start at google.com. Open Google, type your search query, read the results, and follow links by clicking — do not jump directly to any URL, and do not construct or guess URLs from memory or training data.

## Page size management (critical)
Loading large, unfiltered pages makes it hard to locate relevant information and risks exceeding LLM context length limits. Before loading any page, actively try to reduce its size:
- Use the site's search box with specific keywords rather than browsing index pages.
- Apply any available filters: date range, category, author, language, file type, etc.
- Prefer paginated or scoped views over full listing pages.

## Tool selection
- Prefer specialized tools (ArXiv, Wikipedia, YouTube, direct download, etc.) when they directly match the task. Use browser automation only when no dedicated tool fits.
- Only Google Search is permitted as a search engine.
- For academic paper searches, prefer Google Scholar, arXiv, and DBLP.

## Output
- Produce well-structured, detailed output as required. Extract only what is relevant to the task.
- If you use browser tools to save any content, the browser will store it under the directory: [<PROJECT_ROOT>/tmp/browser_wp]. This is enforced by the browser itself — you only need to report the file path in your output when needed.

Work carefully, efficiently, and stay within your assigned retrieval scope.

messages.content:
You are the WebSurfer agent. You retrieve information from the web by navigating and interacting with pages, exactly as a human would.

## Navigation policy
- Unless the user explicitly provides a URL or names a specific website to visit, always start at google.com. Open Google, type your search query, read the results, and follow links by clicking — do not jump directly to any URL, and do not construct or guess URLs from memory or training data.

## Page size management (critical)
Loading large, unfiltered pages makes it hard to locate relevant information and risks exceeding LLM context length limits. Before loading any page, actively try to reduce its size:
- Use the site's search box with specific keywords rather than browsing index pages.
- Apply any available filters: date range, category, author, language, file type, etc.
- Prefer paginated or scoped views over full listing pages.

## Tool selection
- Prefer specialized tools (ArXiv, Wikipedia, YouTube, direct download, etc.) when they directly match the task. Use browser automation only when no dedicated tool fits.
- Only Google Search is permitted as a search engine.
- For academic paper searches, prefer Google Scholar, arXiv, and DBLP.

## Output
- Produce well-structured, detailed output as required. Extract only what is relevant to the task.
- If you use browser tools to save any content, the browser will store it under the directory: [<PROJECT_ROOT>/tmp/browser_wp]. This is enforced by the browser itself — you only need to report the file path in your output when needed.

Work carefully, efficiently, and stay within your assigned retrieval scope.

You are the WebSurfer agent. You retrieve information from the web by navigating and interacting with pages, exactly as a human would.

## Navigation policy
- Unless the user explicitly provides a URL or names a specific website to visit, always start at google.com. Open Google, type your search query, read the results, and follow links by clicking — do not jump directly to any URL, and do not construct or guess URLs from memory or training data.

## Page size management (critical)
Loading large, unfiltered pages makes it hard to locate relevant information and risks exceeding LLM context length limits. Before loading any page, actively try to reduce its size:
- Use the site's search box with specific keywords rather than browsing index pages.
- Apply any available filters: date range, category, author, language, file type, etc.
- Prefer paginated or scoped views over full listing pages.

## Tool selection
- Prefer specialized tools (ArXiv, Wikipedia, YouTube, direct download, etc.) when they directly match the task. Use browser automation only when no dedicated tool fits.
- Only Google Search is permitted as a search engine.
- For academic paper searches, prefer Google Scholar, arXiv, and DBLP.

## Output
- Produce well-structured, detailed output as required. Extract only what is relevant to the task.
- If you use browser tools to save any content, the browser will store it under the directory: [<PROJECT_ROOT>/tmp/browser_wp]. This is enforced by the browser itself — you only need to report the file path in your output when needed.

Work carefully, efficiently, and stay within your assigned retrieval scope.

You are the WebSurfer agent. You retrieve information from the web by navigating and interacting with pages, exactly as a human would.

## Navigation policy
- Unless the user explicitly provides a URL or names a specific website to visit, always start at google.com. Open Google, type your search query, read the results, and follow links by clicking — do not jump directly to any URL, and do not construct or guess URLs from memory or training data.

## Page size management (critical)
Loading large, unfiltered pages makes it hard to locate relevant information and risks exceeding LLM context length limits. Before loading any page, actively try to reduce its size:
- Use the site's search box with specific keywords rather than browsing index pages.
- Apply any available filters: date range, category, author, language, file type, etc.
- Prefer paginated or scoped views over full listing pages.

## Tool selection
- Prefer specialized tools (ArXiv, Wikipedia, YouTube, direct download, etc.) when they directly match the task. Use browser automation only when no dedicated tool fits.
- Only Google Search is permitted as a search engine.
- For academic paper searches, prefer Google Scholar, arXiv, and DBLP.

## Output
- Produce well-structured, detailed output as required. Extract only what is relevant to the task.
- If you use browser tools to save any content, the browser will store it under the directory: [<PROJECT_ROOT>/tmp/browser_wp]. This is enforced by the browser itself — you only need to report the file path in your output when needed.

Work carefully, efficiently, and stay within your assigned retrieval scope.

You are the WebSurfer agent. You retrieve information from the web by navigating and interacting with pages, exactly as a human would.

## Navigation policy
- Unless the user explicitly provides a URL or names a specific website to visit, always start at google.com. Open Google, type your search query, read the results, and follow links by clicking — do not jump directly to any URL, and do not construct or guess URLs from memory or training data.

## Page size management (critical)
Loading large, unfiltered pages makes it hard to locate relevant information and risks exceeding LLM context length limits. Before loading any page, actively try to reduce its size:
- Use the site's search box with specific keywords rather than browsing index pages.
- Apply any available filters: date range, category, author, language, file type, etc.
- Prefer paginated or scoped views over full listing pages.

## Tool selection
- Prefer specialized tools (ArXiv, Wikipedia, YouTube, direct download, etc.) when they directly match the task. Use browser automation only when no dedicated tool fits.
- Only Google Search is permitted as a search engine.
- For academic paper searches, prefer Google Scholar, arXiv, and DBLP.

## Output
- Produce well-structured, detailed output as required. Extract only what is relevant to the task.
- If you use browser tools to save any content, the browser will store it under the directory: [<PROJECT_ROOT>/tmp/browser_wp]. This is enforced by the browser itself — you only need to report the file path in your output when needed.

Work carefully, efficiently, and stay within your assigned retrieval scope.

          - generic [ref=e438]:
            - term [ref=e439]:
              - link "Civility" [ref=e440] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:Civility
            - definition [ref=e441]:
              - text: Rudeness or insensitivity, whether intentional or not, can distract from and interfere with our work.
              - link "Dispute resolution" [ref=e442] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:Dispute_resolution
              - text: forums are available when civil, reasoned discussion breaks down.
            - term [ref=e443]:
              - link "Clean start" [ref=e444] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:Clean_start
            - definition [ref=e445]:
              - text: Any user who is not subject to
              - link "editing sanctions" [ref=e446] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:Sanctions
              - text: may abandon their account and start fresh under a new one, as long as the new account is not used in an
              - link "improper" [ref=e447] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:ILLEGIT
              - text: manner.
            - term [ref=e448]:
              - link "Consensus" [ref=e449] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:Consensus
            - definition [ref=e450]: Consensus among equals is our only tool for resolving content disputes, and our main tool for resolving all other disputes.
            - term [ref=e451]:
              - link "Dispute resolution" [ref=e452] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:Dispute_resolution
            - definition [ref=e453]:
              - text: The first step to resolving any dispute is to
              - emphasis [ref=e454]: talk
              - text: to those who disagree with you. If that fails, there are more structured forms of discussion available.
            - term [ref=e455]:
              - link "Edit warring" [ref=e456] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:Edit_warring
            - definition [ref=e457]:
              - text: If someone challenges your edits, discuss it with them and seek a compromise, or seek
              - link "dispute resolution" [ref=e458] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:DR
              - text: . Do not start fights over competing views and versions.
              - link "Reverting" [ref=e459] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:Revert
              - text: any part of any single page more than three times in twenty-four hours, or even once if long-term edit-warring is apparent, can result in a
              - link "block" [ref=e460] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:BLOCK
              - text: on your account.
            - term [ref=e461]:
              - link "Editing policy" [ref=e462] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:Editing_policy
            - definition [ref=e463]: Improve pages wherever you can, and don't worry about leaving them imperfect. It is advisable to explain major changes.
            - term [ref=e464]:
              - link "Harassment" [ref=e465] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:Harassment
            - definition [ref=e466]: Do not stop other editors from enjoying Wikipedia by making threats, nitpicking good-faith edits to different articles, repeated annoying and unwanted contacts, repeated personal attacks or posting personal information.
            - term [ref=e467]:
              - link "No personal attacks" [ref=e468] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:No_personal_attacks
            - definition [ref=e469]:
              - text: Do not make
              - link "personal attacks" [ref=e470] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Ad_hominem
              - text: anywhere in Wikipedia. Comment on the content, not on the editor. Personal attacks damage the community and deter editors.
            - term [ref=e471]:
              - link "Ownership of content" [ref=e472] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:Ownership_of_content
            - definition [ref=e473]:
              - text: Although you retain some rights under Wikipedia's
              - link "copyright" [ref=e474] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:Copyrights
              - text: provisions, pages that you create and edit belong to the community. Others can and often do mercilessly edit "your" material.
            - term [ref=e475]:
              - link "Sockpuppetry" [ref=e476] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:Sockpuppetry
            - definition [ref=e477]: Do not use multiple accounts to create the illusion of greater support for an issue, to mislead others, or to circumvent a block. Do not ask your friends to create accounts to support you or anyone.
            - term [ref=e478]:
              - link "Username policy" [ref=e479] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:Username_policy
            - definition [ref=e480]:
              - text: Choose a
              - link "neutral username" [ref=e481] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:Username#Inappropriate_usernames
              - text: with which you will be happy. You can usually
              - link "change your name" [ref=e482] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:UNC
              - text: if you need to by asking, but you cannot delete it.
            - term [ref=e483]:
              - link "Vandalism" [ref=e484] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:Vandalism
            - definition [ref=e485]: Vandalism is any addition, deletion, or change to content made in a deliberate attempt to compromise the integrity of the encyclopedia. It is inappropriate behavior for an online encyclopedia.

            - term [ref=e533]:
              - link "Article titles" [ref=e534] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:Article_titles
            - definition [ref=e535]: The ideal title for a Wikipedia article is recognizable to English speakers, easy to find, precise, concise, and consistent with other titles.
            - term [ref=e536]:
              - link "Biographies of living persons" [ref=e537] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:Biographies_of_living_persons
            - definition [ref=e538]: Articles about living persons, which require a degree of sensitivity, must adhere strictly to Wikipedia's content policies. Be very firm about high-quality references, particularly about details of personal lives. Contentious material that is unsourced or poorly sourced should be removed immediately.
            - term [ref=e539]:
              - link "Image use policy" [ref=e540] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:Image_use_policy
            - definition [ref=e541]: Generally avoid uploading non-free images; fully describe images' sources and copyright details on their description pages, and try to make images as useful and reusable as possible.
            - term [ref=e542]:
              - link "Neutral point of view" [ref=e543] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:Neutral_point_of_view
            - definition [ref=e544]:
              - text: Everything that our readers can see, including articles, templates, categories and portals, must be written neutrally and without
              - link "bias" [ref=e545] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:UNDUE
              - text: .
            - term [ref=e546]:
              - link "No original research" [ref=e547] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:No_original_research
            - definition [ref=e548]:
              - text: Articles may not contain any unpublished theories, data, statements, concepts, arguments, or ideas; or any new interpretation, analysis, or synthesis of published data, statements, concepts, arguments, or ideas that, in the words of Wikipedia's co-founder
              - link "Jimbo Wales" [ref=e549] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Jimbo_Wales
              - text: ", would amount to a \"novel narrative or historical interpretation.\""
            - term [ref=e550]:
              - link "Verifiability" [ref=e551] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:Verifiability
            - definition [ref=e552]:
              - text: Articles should
              - link "cite sources" [ref=e553] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:CITE
              - text: whenever possible. While we cannot check the accuracy of cited sources, we can check whether they have been published by a reputable publication and whether independent sources have supported them on review. Any unsourced material may be challenged and removed.
            - term [ref=e554]:
              - link "What Wikipedia is not" [ref=e555] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:What_Wikipedia_is_not
            - definition [ref=e556]:
              - text: Wikipedia is an online

          - generic [ref=e592]:
            - term [ref=e593]:
              - link "Attack page" [ref=e594] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:Attack_page
            - definition [ref=e595]: A Wikipedia article, page, category, redirect or image that exists primarily to disparage its subject is an "attack page". These pages are subject to being deleted by any administrator at any time.
            - term [ref=e596]:
              - link "Criteria for speedy deletion" [ref=e597] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:Criteria_for_speedy_deletion
            - definition [ref=e598]:
              - text: Articles, images, categories etc. may be "speedily deleted" if they clearly fall within certain categories, which generally boil down to pages lacking content, or disruptive pages. Anything potentially controversial should go through the
              - link "deletion process" [ref=e599] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:Articles_for_deletion
              - text: instead.
            - term [ref=e600]:
              - link "Deletion policy" [ref=e601] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:Deletion_policy
            - definition [ref=e602]: Deleting articles requires an administrator and generally follows a consensus-forming process. Most potentially controversial deletions require a three-step process and a waiting period of a week.
            - term [ref=e603]:
              - link "Oversight" [ref=e604] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:Oversight
            - definition [ref=e605]: Content can be hidden from both users and administrators under certain strict criteria.
            - term [ref=e606]:
              - link "Proposed deletion" [ref=e607] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:Proposed_deletion
            - definition [ref=e608]: As a shortcut around the Articles for Deletion ("AfD") process, for uncontroversial deletions an article can be proposed for deletion, but only once. If no one contests the proposed deletion within seven days, an administrator may delete the article.
            - term [ref=e609]:
              - link "Proposed deletion of biographies of living people" [ref=e610] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:Proposed_deletion_of_biographies_of_living_people
            - definition [ref=e611]:
              - text: Articles that are unsourced
              - link "biographies of living persons" [ref=e612] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:Biographies_of_living_persons
              - text: can be proposed for deletion through a special process. If no one contests the proposed deletion within seven days, an administrator may delete the article. In order to contest the proposed deletion, at least one reliable source supporting at least one statement in the article must be added.
            - term [ref=e613]:
              - link "Revision deletion" [ref=e614] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:Revision_deletion
            - definition [ref=e615]: A function available to administrators to eliminate grossly improper posts and log entries.

              - link "Administrators" [ref=e648] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:Administrators
            - definition [ref=e649]: Administrators, like all editors, are not perfect beings. However, in general, they are expected to act as role models within the community, and with a good general standard of civility, fairness, and general conduct both to editors and in content matters. When acting as administrators, they are also expected to be fair, exercise good judgment, and give explanations and be communicative as necessary.
            - term [ref=e650]:
              - link "Banning policy" [ref=e651] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:Banning_policy
            - definition [ref=e652]:
              - text: Extremely disruptive editors may be banned from Wikipedia. Please respect these bans, do not bait banned users, and do not help them out. Bans may be appealed to the
              - link "community" [ref=e653] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:CBAN
              - text: ", the"
              - link "Arbitration Committee" [ref=e654] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:ARBCOM
              - text: ", or the"
              - link "Wikimedia Foundation" [ref=e655] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:WMF
              - text: ", depending on the nature of the ban."
            - term [ref=e656]:
              - link "Blocking policy" [ref=e657] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:Blocking_policy
            - definition [ref=e658]: Disruptive editors can be blocked from editing for short, long, or indefinite periods of time.
            - term [ref=e659]:
              - link "Page protection policy" [ref=e660] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:Protection_policy
            - definition [ref=e661]: Pages can be protected against vandals or during fierce content disputes. Protected pages can, but in general should not, be edited by administrators. In addition, pages undergoing frequent vandalism can be semi-protected to block edits by very new or unregistered editors.

          - generic [ref=e710]:
            - term [ref=e711]:
              - link "Child protection" [ref=e712] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:Child_protection
            - definition [ref=e713]:
              - text: Editors who advocate or attempt to pursue or facilitate inappropriate adult–child relationships, or who identify themselves as
              - link "paedophiles" [ref=e714] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Paedophile
              - text: ", are to be blocked indefinitely."
            - term [ref=e715]:
              - link "Copyright violations" [ref=e716] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:Copyright_violations
            - definition [ref=e717]: Relates to material copied from sources that are neither public domain nor compatibly licensed without the permission of the copyright holder. Wikipedia has no tolerance for copyright violations in our encyclopedia, and we actively strive to find and remove any violations.
            - term [ref=e718]:
              - link "Copyrights" [ref=e719] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:Copyrights
            - definition [ref=e720]: Relates to the copyrighted Wikipedia text being licensed to the public under one or several liberal licenses.
            - term [ref=e721]:
              - link "Libel" [ref=e722] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:Libel
            - definition [ref=e723]:
              - text: It is Wikipedia policy to delete
              - link "libelous" [ref=e724] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Defamation
              - text: revisions from the page history. If you believe you have been defamed, please
              - link "contact us" [ref=e725] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:Contact_us/Article_subjects
              - text: . It is the responsibility of all editors to ensure that material posted on Wikipedia is not
              - link "defamatory" [ref=e726] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Defamation
              - text: .
            - term [ref=e727]:
              - link "No legal threats" [ref=e728] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:No_legal_threats
            - definition [ref=e729]:
              - text: Use
              - link "dispute resolution" [ref=e730] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:Dispute_resolution
              - text: rather than making legal threats, for everyone's sake, as we respond quickly to complaints of defamation or copyright infringement. If you make legal threats, or take legal action over a Wikipedia dispute, you will be
              - link "blocked" [ref=e731] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:Blocking_policy
              - text: from editing, so that the matter is not exacerbated through other channels. If you do take legal action, please refrain from editing until it is resolved.
            - term [ref=e732]:
              - link "Non-free content criteria" [ref=e733] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:Non-free_content_criteria
            - definition [ref=e734]: The Exemption Doctrine Policy for the English Wikipedia. The cases in which you can declare usage of a non-free image, audio clip, or video clip as "fair use" are quite narrow. You must specify the exact use, and only use the image or clip in that one context. Only use non-free content as a last resort.
            - term [ref=e735]:
              - link "Paid-contribution disclosure" [ref=e736] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:Paid-contribution_disclosure
            - definition [ref=e737]: Editors must disclose their employer, client, and affiliation with respect to any contribution for which they receive, or expect to receive, compensation.
            - term [ref=e738]:
              - link "Reusing Wikipedia content" [ref=e739] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:Reusing_Wikipedia_content
            - definition [ref=e740]:
              - text: Relates to the basis of using Wikipedia content in your own publications. Most of Wikipedia's material may be freely used under the
              - link "CC BY-SA" [ref=e741] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/CC_BY-SA
              - text: and
              - link "GFDL" [ref=e742] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/GNU_Free_Documentation_License
              - text: licences. Which means you must credit the authors, re-license the material under CC BY-SA or GFDL, and allow free access to it.
            - term [ref=e743]:
              - link "Terms of use" [ref=e744] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:Terms_of_use
            - definition [ref=e745]:
              - text: The terms of use are established by the
              - link "Wikimedia Foundation" [ref=e746] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikimedia_Foundation
              - text: .

                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:Bot_policy
            - definition [ref=e762]: Programs that update pages automatically in a useful and harmless way may be welcome, as long as their owners seek approval first and are careful to keep them from running amok or being a drain on resources.
            - term [ref=e763]:
              - link "CheckUser" [ref=e764] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:CheckUser
            - definition [ref=e765]: CheckUser is a tool allowed to be used by a small number of editors who are permitted to examine user IP information and other server log data under certain circumstances, for the purposes of protecting Wikipedia against actual and potential disruption and abuse.
            - term [ref=e766]:
              - link "Edit filter manager" [ref=e767] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:Edit_filter_manager
            - definition [ref=e768]: Edit filter manager is a user group that allows users to view and edit the details and code of edit filters, as well as view the logs of such filters, including private filters.
            - term [ref=e769]:
              - link "Edit filter helper" [ref=e770] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:Edit_filter_helper
            - definition [ref=e771]: Edit filter helper is a user group that allows non-administrators to view the details, code, and logs of private edit filters, but not to edit them.
            - term [ref=e772]:
              - link "Event coordinator" [ref=e773] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:Event_coordinator
            - definition [ref=e774]:
              - text: The event coordinator user group allows users to create new accounts without limits, and to temporarily add the
              - link "confirmed" [ref=e776] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:Confirmed_users
              - text: user right to new accounts.
            - term [ref=e777]:
              - link "Global rights policy" [ref=e778] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:Global_rights_policy
            - definition [ref=e779]:
              - text: English Wikipedia restrictions on users who have global rights on all
              - link "Foundation" [ref=e780] [cursor=pointer]:

              - text: sites
            - term [ref=e781]:
              - link "Interface administrators" [ref=e782] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:Interface_administrators
            - definition [ref=e783]: Interface administrators are users who can edit all scripts and style pages in the MediaWiki namespace.
            - term [ref=e784]:
              - link "IP block exemption" [ref=e785] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:IP_block_exemption
            - definition [ref=e786]: Editors in good standing whose editing is disrupted by unrelated blocks or firewalls may request IP block exemption, which allows editing on an otherwise-blocked IP address.
            - term [ref=e787]:
              - link "Open proxies" [ref=e788] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:Open_proxies
            - definition [ref=e789]:
              - link "Open proxies" [ref=e790] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Open_proxy
              - text: may be blocked from editing for any period at any time to deal with editing abuse.
            - term [ref=e791]:
              - link "Page mover" [ref=e792] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:Page_mover
            - definition [ref=e793]: The page mover permission allows editors to move pages, and subpages, without leaving redirects.
            - term [ref=e794]:
              - link "Policies and guidelines" [ref=e795] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:Policies_and_guidelines
            - definition [ref=e796]: Understanding and changing policies and guidelines
            - term [ref=e797]:

            - definition [ref=e799]:
              - text: The temporary account IP viewer permission grants the ability to view the underlying IP addresses of
              - link "temporary accounts" [ref=e800] [cursor=pointer]:

              - text: ", a system introduced to replace IP editing."
            - term [ref=e801]:
              - link "Volunteer response team" [ref=e802] [cursor=pointer]:

            - definition [ref=e803]:
              - text: If you disagree with an edit that was made referencing a volunteer response ticket number as a reason, or in the edit summary, please follow the steps listed at "
              - link "Wikipedia:Volunteer response team#Dispute resolution" [ref=e804] [cursor=pointer]:

              - text: "\"."

messages.content:
You are the WebSurfer agent. You retrieve information from the web by navigating and interacting with pages, exactly as a human would.

## Navigation policy
- Unless the user explicitly provides a URL or names a specific website to visit, always start at google.com. Open Google, type your search query, read the results, and follow links by clicking — do not jump directly to any URL, and do not construct or guess URLs from memory or training data.

          - generic [ref=e438]:
            - term [ref=e439]:
              - link "Civility" [ref=e440] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:Civility
            - definition [ref=e441]:
              - text: Rudeness or insensitivity, whether intentional or not, can distract from and interfere with our work.
              - link "Dispute resolution" [ref=e442] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:Dispute_resolution
              - text: forums are available when civil, reasoned discussion breaks down.
            - term [ref=e443]:
              - link "Clean start" [ref=e444] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:Clean_start
            - definition [ref=e445]:
              - text: Any user who is not subject to
              - link "editing sanctions" [ref=e446] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:Sanctions
              - text: may abandon their account and start fresh under a new one, as long as the new account is not used in an
              - link "improper" [ref=e447] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:ILLEGIT
              - text: manner.
            - term [ref=e448]:
              - link "Consensus" [ref=e449] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:Consensus
            - definition [ref=e450]: Consensus among equals is our only tool for resolving content disputes, and our main tool for resolving all other disputes.
            - term [ref=e451]:
              - link "Dispute resolution" [ref=e452] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:Dispute_resolution
            - definition [ref=e453]:
              - text: The first step to resolving any dispute is to
              - emphasis [ref=e454]: talk
              - text: to those who disagree with you. If that fails, there are more structured forms of discussion available.
            - term [ref=e455]:
              - link "Edit warring" [ref=e456] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:Edit_warring
            - definition [ref=e457]:
              - text: If someone challenges your edits, discuss it with them and seek a compromise, or seek
              - link "dispute resolution" [ref=e458] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:DR
              - text: . Do not start fights over competing views and versions.
              - link "Reverting" [ref=e459] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:Revert
              - text: any part of any single page more than three times in twenty-four hours, or even once if long-term edit-warring is apparent, can result in a
              - link "block" [ref=e460] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:BLOCK
              - text: on your account.
            - term [ref=e461]:
              - link "Editing policy" [ref=e462] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:Editing_policy
            - definition [ref=e463]: Improve pages wherever you can, and don't worry about leaving them imperfect. It is advisable to explain major changes.
            - term [ref=e464]:
              - link "Harassment" [ref=e465] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:Harassment
            - definition [ref=e466]: Do not stop other editors from enjoying Wikipedia by making threats, nitpicking good-faith edits to different articles, repeated annoying and unwanted contacts, repeated personal attacks or posting personal information.
            - term [ref=e467]:
              - link "No personal attacks" [ref=e468] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:No_personal_attacks
            - definition [ref=e469]:
              - text: Do not make
              - link "personal attacks" [ref=e470] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Ad_hominem
              - text: anywhere in Wikipedia. Comment on the content, not on the editor. Personal attacks damage the community and deter editors.
            - term [ref=e471]:
              - link "Ownership of content" [ref=e472] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:Ownership_of_content
            - definition [ref=e473]:
              - text: Although you retain some rights under Wikipedia's
              - link "copyright" [ref=e474] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:Copyrights
              - text: provisions, pages that you create and edit belong to the community. Others can and often do mercilessly edit "your" material.
            - term [ref=e475]:
              - link "Sockpuppetry" [ref=e476] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:Sockpuppetry
            - definition [ref=e477]: Do not use multiple accounts to create the illusion of greater support for an issue, to mislead others, or to circumvent a block. Do not ask your friends to create accounts to support you or anyone.
            - term [ref=e478]:
              - link "Username policy" [ref=e479] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:Username_policy
            - definition [ref=e480]:
              - text: Choose a
              - link "neutral username" [ref=e481] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:Username#Inappropriate_usernames
              - text: with which you will be happy. You can usually
              - link "change your name" [ref=e482] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:UNC
              - text: if you need to by asking, but you cannot delete it.
            - term [ref=e483]:
              - link "Vandalism" [ref=e484] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:Vandalism
            - definition [ref=e485]: Vandalism is any addition, deletion, or change to content made in a deliberate attempt to compromise the integrity of the encyclopedia. It is inappropriate behavior for an online encyclopedia.

            - term [ref=e533]:
              - link "Article titles" [ref=e534] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:Article_titles
            - definition [ref=e535]: The ideal title for a Wikipedia article is recognizable to English speakers, easy to find, precise, concise, and consistent with other titles.
            - term [ref=e536]:
              - link "Biographies of living persons" [ref=e537] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:Biographies_of_living_persons
            - definition [ref=e538]: Articles about living persons, which require a degree of sensitivity, must adhere strictly to Wikipedia's content policies. Be very firm about high-quality references, particularly about details of personal lives. Contentious material that is unsourced or poorly sourced should be removed immediately.
            - term [ref=e539]:
              - link "Image use policy" [ref=e540] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:Image_use_policy
            - definition [ref=e541]: Generally avoid uploading non-free images; fully describe images' sources and copyright details on their description pages, and try to make images as useful and reusable as possible.
            - term [ref=e542]:
              - link "Neutral point of view" [ref=e543] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:Neutral_point_of_view
            - definition [ref=e544]:
              - text: Everything that our readers can see, including articles, templates, categories and portals, must be written neutrally and without
              - link "bias" [ref=e545] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:UNDUE
              - text: .
            - term [ref=e546]:
              - link "No original research" [ref=e547] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:No_original_research
            - definition [ref=e548]:
              - text: Articles may not contain any unpublished theories, data, statements, concepts, arguments, or ideas; or any new interpretation, analysis, or synthesis of published data, statements, concepts, arguments, or ideas that, in the words of Wikipedia's co-founder
              - link "Jimbo Wales" [ref=e549] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Jimbo_Wales
              - text: ", would amount to a \"novel narrative or historical interpretation.\""
            - term [ref=e550]:
              - link "Verifiability" [ref=e551] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:Verifiability
            - definition [ref=e552]:
              - text: Articles should
              - link "cite sources" [ref=e553] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:CITE
              - text: whenever possible. While we cannot check the accuracy of cited sources, we can check whether they have been published by a reputable publication and whether independent sources have supported them on review. Any unsourced material may be challenged and removed.
            - term [ref=e554]:
              - link "What Wikipedia is not" [ref=e555] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:What_Wikipedia_is_not
            - definition [ref=e556]:
              - text: Wikipedia is an online
              - link "encyclopedia" [ref=e557] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Encyclopedia
              - text: . Please avoid using Wikipedia for other purposes.

          - generic [ref=e592]:
            - term [ref=e593]:
              - link "Attack page" [ref=e594] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:Attack_page
            - definition [ref=e595]: A Wikipedia article, page, category, redirect or image that exists primarily to disparage its subject is an "attack page". These pages are subject to being deleted by any administrator at any time.
            - term [ref=e596]:
              - link "Criteria for speedy deletion" [ref=e597] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:Criteria_for_speedy_deletion
            - definition [ref=e598]:
              - text: Articles, images, categories etc. may be "speedily deleted" if they clearly fall within certain categories, which generally boil down to pages lacking content, or disruptive pages. Anything potentially controversial should go through the
              - link "deletion process" [ref=e599] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:Articles_for_deletion
              - text: instead.
            - term [ref=e600]:
              - link "Deletion policy" [ref=e601] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:Deletion_policy
            - definition [ref=e602]: Deleting articles requires an administrator and generally follows a consensus-forming process. Most potentially controversial deletions require a three-step process and a waiting period of a week.
            - term [ref=e603]:
              - link "Oversight" [ref=e604] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:Oversight
            - definition [ref=e605]: Content can be hidden from both users and administrators under certain strict criteria.
            - term [ref=e606]:
              - link "Proposed deletion" [ref=e607] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:Proposed_deletion
            - definition [ref=e608]: As a shortcut around the Articles for Deletion ("AfD") process, for uncontroversial deletions an article can be proposed for deletion, but only once. If no one contests the proposed deletion within seven days, an administrator may delete the article.
            - term [ref=e609]:
              - link "Proposed deletion of biographies of living people" [ref=e610] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:Proposed_deletion_of_biographies_of_living_people
            - definition [ref=e611]:
              - text: Articles that are unsourced
              - link "biographies of living persons" [ref=e612] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:Biographies_of_living_persons
              - text: can be proposed for deletion through a special process. If no one contests the proposed deletion within seven days, an administrator may delete the article. In order to contest the proposed deletion, at least one reliable source supporting at least one statement in the article must be added.
            - term [ref=e613]:
              - link "Revision deletion" [ref=e614] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:Revision_deletion
            - definition [ref=e615]: A function available to administrators to eliminate grossly improper posts and log entries.

          - generic [ref=e646]:
            - term [ref=e647]:
              - link "Administrators" [ref=e648] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:Administrators
            - definition [ref=e649]: Administrators, like all editors, are not perfect beings. However, in general, they are expected to act as role models within the community, and with a good general standard of civility, fairness, and general conduct both to editors and in content matters. When acting as administrators, they are also expected to be fair, exercise good judgment, and give explanations and be communicative as necessary.
            - term [ref=e650]:
              - link "Banning policy" [ref=e651] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:Banning_policy
            - definition [ref=e652]:
              - text: Extremely disruptive editors may be banned from Wikipedia. Please respect these bans, do not bait banned users, and do not help them out. Bans may be appealed to the
              - link "community" [ref=e653] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:CBAN
              - text: ", the"
              - link "Arbitration Committee" [ref=e654] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:ARBCOM
              - text: ", or the"
              - link "Wikimedia Foundation" [ref=e655] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:WMF
              - text: ", depending on the nature of the ban."
            - term [ref=e656]:
              - link "Blocking policy" [ref=e657] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:Blocking_policy
            - definition [ref=e658]: Disruptive editors can be blocked from editing for short, long, or indefinite periods of time.
            - term [ref=e659]:
              - link "Page protection policy" [ref=e660] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:Protection_policy
            - definition [ref=e661]: Pages can be protected against vandals or during fierce content disputes. Protected pages can, but in general should not, be edited by administrators. In addition, pages undergoing frequent vandalism can be semi-protected to block edits by very new or unregistered editors.

            - text: These are policies with

            - text: . Legal issues are raised by filing a formal complaint with the Wikimedia Foundation.
          - generic [ref=e710]:
            - term [ref=e711]:
              - link "Child protection" [ref=e712] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:Child_protection
            - definition [ref=e713]:
              - text: Editors who advocate or attempt to pursue or facilitate inappropriate adult–child relationships, or who identify themselves as
              - link "paedophiles" [ref=e714] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Paedophile
              - text: ", are to be blocked indefinitely."
            - term [ref=e715]:
              - link "Copyright violations" [ref=e716] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:Copyright_violations
            - definition [ref=e717]: Relates to material copied from sources that are neither public domain nor compatibly licensed without the permission of the copyright holder. Wikipedia has no tolerance for copyright violations in our encyclopedia, and we actively strive to find and remove any violations.
            - term [ref=e718]:
              - link "Copyrights" [ref=e719] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:Copyrights
            - definition [ref=e720]: Relates to the copyrighted Wikipedia text being licensed to the public under one or several liberal licenses.
            - term [ref=e721]:
              - link "Libel" [ref=e722] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:Libel
            - definition [ref=e723]:
              - text: It is Wikipedia policy to delete
              - link "libelous" [ref=e724] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Defamation
              - text: revisions from the page history. If you believe you have been defamed, please
              - link "contact us" [ref=e725] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:Contact_us/Article_subjects
              - text: . It is the responsibility of all editors to ensure that material posted on Wikipedia is not
              - link "defamatory" [ref=e726] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Defamation
              - text: .
            - term [ref=e727]:
              - link "No legal threats" [ref=e728] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:No_legal_threats
            - definition [ref=e729]:
              - text: Use
              - link "dispute resolution" [ref=e730] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:Dispute_resolution
              - text: rather than making legal threats, for everyone's sake, as we respond quickly to complaints of defamation or copyright infringement. If you make legal threats, or take legal action over a Wikipedia dispute, you will be
              - link "blocked" [ref=e731] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:Blocking_policy
              - text: from editing, so that the matter is not exacerbated through other channels. If you do take legal action, please refrain from editing until it is resolved.
            - term [ref=e732]:
              - link "Non-free content criteria" [ref=e733] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:Non-free_content_criteria
            - definition [ref=e734]: The Exemption Doctrine Policy for the English Wikipedia. The cases in which you can declare usage of a non-free image, audio clip, or video clip as "fair use" are quite narrow. You must specify the exact use, and only use the image or clip in that one context. Only use non-free content as a last resort.
            - term [ref=e735]:
              - link "Paid-contribution disclosure" [ref=e736] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:Paid-contribution_disclosure
            - definition [ref=e737]: Editors must disclose their employer, client, and affiliation with respect to any contribution for which they receive, or expect to receive, compensation.
            - term [ref=e738]:
              - link "Reusing Wikipedia content" [ref=e739] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:Reusing_Wikipedia_content
            - definition [ref=e740]:
              - text: Relates to the basis of using Wikipedia content in your own publications. Most of Wikipedia's material may be freely used under the
              - link "CC BY-SA" [ref=e741] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/CC_BY-SA
              - text: and
              - link "GFDL" [ref=e742] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/GNU_Free_Documentation_License
              - text: licences. Which means you must credit the authors, re-license the material under CC BY-SA or GFDL, and allow free access to it.
            - term [ref=e743]:
              - link "Terms of use" [ref=e744] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:Terms_of_use
            - definition [ref=e745]:
              - text: The terms of use are established by the
              - link "Wikimedia Foundation" [ref=e746] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikimedia_Foundation
              - text: .

              - link "Bot policy" [ref=e761] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:Bot_policy
            - definition [ref=e762]: Programs that update pages automatically in a useful and harmless way may be welcome, as long as their owners seek approval first and are careful to keep them from running amok or being a drain on resources.
            - term [ref=e763]:
              - link "CheckUser" [ref=e764] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:CheckUser
            - definition [ref=e765]: CheckUser is a tool allowed to be used by a small number of editors who are permitted to examine user IP information and other server log data under certain circumstances, for the purposes of protecting Wikipedia against actual and potential disruption and abuse.
            - term [ref=e766]:
              - link "Edit filter manager" [ref=e767] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:Edit_filter_manager
            - definition [ref=e768]: Edit filter manager is a user group that allows users to view and edit the details and code of edit filters, as well as view the logs of such filters, including private filters.
            - term [ref=e769]:
              - link "Edit filter helper" [ref=e770] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:Edit_filter_helper
            - definition [ref=e771]: Edit filter helper is a user group that allows non-administrators to view the details, code, and logs of private edit filters, but not to edit them.
            - term [ref=e772]:
              - link "Event coordinator" [ref=e773] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:Event_coordinator
            - definition [ref=e774]:
              - text: The event coordinator user group allows users to create new accounts without limits, and to temporarily add the
              - link "confirmed" [ref=e776] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:Confirmed_users
              - text: user right to new accounts.
            - term [ref=e777]:
              - link "Global rights policy" [ref=e778] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:Global_rights_policy
            - definition [ref=e779]:
              - text: English Wikipedia restrictions on users who have global rights on all
              - link "Foundation" [ref=e780] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: https://meta.wikimedia.org/wiki/
              - text: sites
            - term [ref=e781]:
              - link "Interface administrators" [ref=e782] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:Interface_administrators
            - definition [ref=e783]: Interface administrators are users who can edit all scripts and style pages in the MediaWiki namespace.
            - term [ref=e784]:
              - link "IP block exemption" [ref=e785] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:IP_block_exemption
            - definition [ref=e786]: Editors in good standing whose editing is disrupted by unrelated blocks or firewalls may request IP block exemption, which allows editing on an otherwise-blocked IP address.
            - term [ref=e787]:
              - link "Open proxies" [ref=e788] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:Open_proxies
            - definition [ref=e789]:
              - link "Open proxies" [ref=e790] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Open_proxy
              - text: may be blocked from editing for any period at any time to deal with editing abuse.
            - term [ref=e791]:
              - link "Page mover" [ref=e792] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:Page_mover
            - definition [ref=e793]: The page mover permission allows editors to move pages, and subpages, without leaving redirects.
            - term [ref=e794]:
              - link "Policies and guidelines" [ref=e795] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:Policies_and_guidelines
            - definition [ref=e796]: Understanding and changing policies and guidelines
            - term [ref=e797]:
              - link "Temporary account IP viewer" [ref=e798] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:Temporary_account_IP_viewer
            - definition [ref=e799]:
              - text: The temporary account IP viewer permission grants the ability to view the underlying IP addresses of
              - link "temporary accounts" [ref=e800] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:TA
              - text: ", a system introduced to replace IP editing."
            - term [ref=e801]:
              - link "Volunteer response team" [ref=e802] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:Volunteer_response_team
            - definition [ref=e803]:
              - text: If you disagree with an edit that was made referencing a volunteer response ticket number as a reason, or in the edit summary, please follow the steps listed at "
              - link "Wikipedia:Volunteer response team#Dispute resolution" [ref=e804] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:Volunteer_response_team#Dispute_resolution
              - text: "\"."
            - term [ref=e805]:
              - link "Wikimedia policy" [ref=e806] [cursor=pointer]:

            - definition [ref=e807]:

            - link "Wikipedia" [ref=e267] [cursor=pointer]:

            - text: "'s content is governed by three principal core"

            - listitem [ref=e273]:
              - text: Neutral point of view (
              - link "WP:NPOV" [ref=e274] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:NPOV
              - text: ) – All Wikipedia articles and other encyclopedic content must be written from a
              - emphasis [ref=e275]: neutral point of view
              - text: ", representing significant views fairly, proportionately and without bias."
            - listitem [ref=e276]:
              - text: Verifiability (
              - link "WP:V" [ref=e277] [cursor=pointer]:

              - text: ) – Material challenged or
              - link "likely to be challenged" [ref=e278] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:LIKELY
              - text: ", and all quotations, must be attributed to a reliable, published source. In Wikipedia, verifiability means that people reading and editing the encyclopedia can check that information comes from a"

              - link "WP:NOR" [ref=e281] [cursor=pointer]:

              - text: ) – Wikipedia does
              - link "not" [ref=e282] [cursor=pointer]:

              - link "reliable, published source" [ref=e283] [cursor=pointer]:

            - text: upon which these policy statements are based are not superseded by other policies or guidelines, or by editors' consensus. These three policy pages may be edited only to improve the application and explanation of the principles.

          - paragraph [ref=e301]:
            - text: "\""
            - link "No original research" [ref=e302] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:NOR
            - text: "\" (NOR) has its origins in the \""
            - link "neutral point of view" [ref=e303] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:NPOV
            - text: "\" (NPOV) policy and the problem of dealing with"
            - link "undue weight" [ref=e304] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:DUE
            - text: and
            - link "fringe theories" [ref=e305] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:Fringe_theories
            - text: . The core policy of Wikipedia, NPOV, is meant to provide a framework whereby editors with diverse, often conflicting, even opposing points of view can collaborate on the creation of an encyclopedia. It does so through the principle that while it is often hard for people to agree as to what is the truth, it is much easier for people to agree as to what they and others
            - emphasis [ref=e306]: believe
            - text: to be the truth. Therefore, Wikipedia does not use "truth" as a criterion for inclusion. Instead, it aims to account for different, notable views of the truth. First codified in
            - link "February 2001" [ref=e307] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: http://web.archive.org/web/20160418185834/http://cyber.law.harvard.edu/~reagle/wp-redux/NeutralPointOfView/982358834.html
            - text: ", the objective of the NPOV policy is to produce an unbiased encyclopedia."
          - paragraph [ref=e308]:
            - text: In the two years that followed, a good deal of conflict on article talk pages involved accusations that editors were violating NPOV, and it became clear that this policy, which provided a philosophical foundation for Wikipedia, needed to be supplemented. Wikipedians developed the concept of "
            - link "verifiability" [ref=e309] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:V
            - text: "\" (V) as a way of ensuring the accuracy of articles by encouraging editors to cite sources; this concept was"
            - link "established as a policy in August 2003" [ref=e310] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Wikipedia:Verifiability&oldid=1339095
            - text: . Verifiability was also promoted as a way to ensure that
            - emphasis [ref=e311]: notable
            - text: views would be represented, under the assumption that the most notable views were easiest to document with sources. Notability is especially important because while NPOV encourages editors to add alternate and multiple points of view to an article, it does not claim that all views are equal. Although NPOV does not claim that some views are more truthful than others, it does acknowledge that some views are held by more people than others. Accurately representing a view therefore also means explaining who holds the view and whether it is a majority or minority view.
          - paragraph [ref=e312]:
            - text: Soon it became evident that editors who rejected a majority view would often marshal sources to argue that a minority view was superior to a majority view—or would even add sources in order to promote the editor's own view. Therefore, the
            - link "NOR policy was established in 2003" [ref=e313] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Wikipedia:No_original_research&oldid=2014449
            - text: to address problematic uses of sources. The original motivation for NOR was to prevent editors from introducing fringe views in science, especially physics—or from excluding verifiable views that, in the judgement of editors, were incorrect.
            - superscript [ref=e314]:
              - link "[1]" [ref=e315] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-1"
            - text: It soon became clear that the policy should apply to any editor trying to introduce their own views into an article. This also led to the refinement and creation of sub sections dealing with the
            - link "balance of coverage" [ref=e316] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:DUE
            - text: .
          - paragraph [ref=e317]: "In its earliest form, the policy singled out edits for exclusion that:"
          - list [ref=e318]:
            - listitem [ref=e319]: Introduce a theory or method of solution;
            - listitem [ref=e320]: Introduce original ideas;
            - listitem [ref=e321]:
              - text: Define existing terms in different ways; or introduce
              - link "neologisms" [ref=e322] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Neologism
              - text: ;
          - paragraph [ref=e323]: "and established as criteria for inclusion edits that present:"
          - list [ref=e324]:
            - listitem [ref=e325]: Ideas that have been accepted for publication in a peer-reviewed journal; or
            - listitem [ref=e326]:
              - text: "Ideas that have become newsworthy: they have been repeatedly and independently reported in newspapers or news stories (such as the"
              - link "cold fusion" [ref=e327] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Cold_fusion
              - text: story).
          - paragraph [ref=e328]:
            - text: As a more diverse community of editors were drawn to Wikipedia, it became clear that other topics besides physics, such as politics, religion, and history, were attracting original research. The need arose to seek a more systematic approach to define original research and guide editors to avoid it.
            - superscript [ref=e329]:
              - link "[2]" [ref=e330] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-2"
            - text: The principles of "verifiability" and "no original research" overlap, and an attempt was made in 2007 to combine the two pages into one (see
            - link "Wikipedia:Attribution" [ref=e331] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:Attribution
            - text: ), but it failed to gain consensus.

                - text: "Wikipedia's co-founder, Jimmy Wales, has described the original research policy as originating \"primarily as a practical means to deal with physics cranks, of which of course there are a number on the web. messages.content:
You are the WebSurfer agent. You retrieve information from the web by navigating and interacting with pages, exactly as a human would.

## Navigation policy
- Unless the user explicitly provides a URL or names a specific website to visit, always start at google.com. Open Google, type your search query, read the results, and follow links by clicking — do not jump directly to any URL, and do not construct or guess URLs from memory or training data.

## Page size management (critical)
Loading large, unfiltered pages makes it hard to locate relevant information and risks exceeding LLM context length limits. Before loading any page, actively try to reduce its size:
- Use the site's search box with specific keywords rather than browsing index pages.
- Apply any available filters: date range, category, author, language, file type, etc.
- Prefer paginated or scoped views over full listing pages.

## Tool selection
- Prefer specialized tools (ArXiv, Wikipedia, YouTube, direct download, etc.) when they directly match the task. Use browser automation only when no dedicated tool fits.
- Only Google Search is permitted as a search engine.
- For academic paper searches, prefer Google Scholar, arXiv, and DBLP.

## Output
- Produce well-structured, detailed output as required. Extract only what is relevant to the task.
- If you use browser tools to save any content, the browser will store it under the directory: [<PROJECT_ROOT>/tmp/browser_wp]. This is enforced by the browser itself — you only need to report the file path in your output when needed.

Work carefully, efficiently, and stay within your assigned retrieval scope.

              - link "Reverting" [ref=e459] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:Revert
              - text: any part of any single page more than three times in twenty-four hours, or even once if long-term edit-warring is apparent, can result in a
              - link "block" [ref=e460] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:BLOCK
              - text: on your account.
            - term [ref=e461]:
              - link "Editing policy" [ref=e462] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:Editing_policy
            - definition [ref=e463]: Improve pages wherever you can, and don't worry about leaving them imperfect. It is advisable to explain major changes.
            - term [ref=e464]:
              - link "Harassment" [ref=e465] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:Harassment
            - definition [ref=e466]: Do not stop other editors from enjoying Wikipedia by making threats, nitpicking good-faith edits to different articles, repeated annoying and unwanted contacts, repeated personal attacks or posting personal information.
            - term [ref=e467]:
              - link "No personal attacks" [ref=e468] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:No_personal_attacks
            - definition [ref=e469]:
              - text: Do not make
              - link "personal attacks" [ref=e470] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Ad_hominem
              - text: anywhere in Wikipedia. Comment on the content, not on the editor. Personal attacks damage the community and deter editors.
            - term [ref=e471]:
              - link "Ownership of content" [ref=e472] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:Ownership_of_content
            - definition [ref=e473]:
              - text: Although you retain some rights under Wikipedia's
              - link "copyright" [ref=e474] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:Copyrights
              - text: provisions, pages that you create and edit belong to the community. Others can and often do mercilessly edit "your" material.
            - term [ref=e475]:
              - link "Sockpuppetry" [ref=e476] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:Sockpuppetry
            - definition [ref=e477]: Do not use multiple accounts to create the illusion of greater support for an issue, to mislead others, or to circumvent a block. Do not ask your friends to create accounts to support you or anyone.
            - term [ref=e478]:
              - link "Username policy" [ref=e479] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:Username_policy
            - definition [ref=e480]:
              - text: Choose a
              - link "neutral username" [ref=e481] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:Username#Inappropriate_usernames
              - text: with which you will be happy. You can usually
              - link "change your name" [ref=e482] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:UNC
              - text: if you need to by asking, but you cannot delete it.
            - term [ref=e483]:
              - link "Vandalism" [ref=e484] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:Vandalism
            - definition [ref=e485]: Vandalism is any addition, deletion, or change to content made in a deliberate attempt to compromise the integrity of the encyclopedia. It is inappropriate behavior for an online encyclopedia.
