            - link "Black bean aphids" [ref=e524] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Black_bean_aphid
            - text: are a serious pest to broad beans and other beans. Common hosts for this pest are fathen, thistle and dock.

            - text: and
            - link "bean weevil" [ref=e526] [cursor=pointer]:

          - paragraph [ref=e567]:

            - text: ", and peas show that they last about 5 years in storage. Environmental factors that are important in influencing germination are relative humidity and temperature.               - link "[36]" [ref=e754] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-b1-47"
            - text: The soybean was domesticated around 5,000 years ago in China from a descendant of the wild vine Glycine soja.
            - superscript [ref=e755]:
              - link "[37]" [ref=e756] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-48"
          - paragraph [ref=e757]:
            - text: The oldest-known domesticated beans in the Americas were found in
            - link "Guitarrero Cave" [ref=e758] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Guitarrero_Cave
            - text: ", an archaeological site in"
            - link "Peru" [ref=e759] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Peru
            - text: ", and dated to around the second millennium BCE."
            - superscript [ref=e760]:
              - link "[38]" [ref=e761] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-Chazan-49"
            - text: Genetic analyses of the common bean Phaseolus show that it originated in
            - link "Mesoamerica" [ref=e762] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Mesoamerica
            - text: ", and subsequently spread southward, along with"
            - link "maize" [ref=e763] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Maize
            - text: and squash, traditional companion crops.
            - superscript [ref=e764]:
              - link "[39]" [ref=e765] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-50"
            - text: In the United States, the domesticated soybean was introduced in 1770 by
            - link "Benjamin Franklin" [ref=e766] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Benjamin_Franklin
            - text: after he sent seeds to Philadelphia from France.
            - superscript [ref=e767]:
              - link "[40]" [ref=e768] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-51"

          - paragraph [ref=e780]:
            - text: The International Year of Pulses 2016 was declared by the
            - link "Sixty-eighth session of the United Nations General Assembly" [ref=e781] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Sixty-eighth_session_of_the_United_Nations_General_Assembly
            - text: .
            - superscript [ref=e782]:
              - link "[41]" [ref=e783] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-iyp-52"
            - text: The
            - link "Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations" [ref=e784] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Food_and_Agriculture_Organization_of_the_United_Nations
            - text: was nominated to facilitate the implementation of the year in collaboration with governments, relevant organizations, non-governmental organizations and other relevant stakeholders. Its aim was to heighten public awareness of the nutritional benefits of pulses as part of
            - link "sustainable food" [ref=e785] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Sustainable_food_systems
            - text: production aimed towards
            - link "food security" [ref=e786] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Food_security
            - text: and
            - link "nutrition" [ref=e787] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Nutrition
            - text: . The year created an opportunity to encourage connections throughout the food chain that would better use pulse-based proteins, further global production of pulses, better use
            - link "crop rotations" [ref=e788] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Crop_rotation
            - text: and address challenges in the global trade of pulses.

            - text: are one exception to this rule). These bacteria have the special ability of
            - link "fixing nitrogen" [ref=e452] [cursor=pointer]:

          - paragraph [ref=e480]:
            - text: This arrangement means that the root nodules are sources of nitrogen for legumes, making them relatively rich in nitrogenous

            - text: and

            - link "ingredient" [ref=e483] [cursor=pointer]:

            - text: in the production of proteins.
          - paragraph [ref=e484]:
            - text: When a legume plant dies in the field, for example following the
            - link "harvest" [ref=e485] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Harvest
            - text: ", all of its remaining nitrogen, incorporated into"
            - link "amino acids" [ref=e486] [cursor=pointer]:

            - text: inside the remaining plant parts, is released back into the soil. In the soil, the amino acids are converted to nitrate (
            - generic [ref=e487]:
              - text: "NO"
              - generic [ref=e488]:
                - generic [ref=e489]: −
                - generic [ref=e490]: "3"
            - text: ), making the nitrogen available to other plants, thereby serving as fertilizer for future crops.
            - superscript [ref=e491]:

            - superscript [ref=e493]:

          - paragraph [ref=e500]:
            - text: In many traditional and
            - link "organic farming" [ref=e501] [cursor=pointer]:

            - text: practices,

            - text: or
            - link "polyculture" [ref=e503] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Polyculture
            - text: involving legumes is common. By alternating between legumes and non-legumes, or by growing both together for part of the growing season, the field can receive a sufficient amount of nitrogenous compounds to produce a good result without adding nitrogenous fertilizer. Legumes are often used as
            - link "green manure" [ref=e504] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Green_manure
            - text: .
            - superscript [ref=e505]:
              - text: "["
              - link "citation needed" [ref=e507] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed
              - text: "]"
          - paragraph [ref=e508]:
            - text: Sri Lanka developed the
            - link "polyculture" [ref=e509] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Polyculture
            - text: practice known as coconut-soybean
            - link "intercropping" [ref=e510] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Intercropping
            - text: ". Grain legumes are grown in coconut (Cocos nuficera) groves in two ways: intercropping or as a cash crop. These are grown mainly for their protein, vegetable oil and ability to uphold soil fertility."
            - superscript [ref=e511]:
              - link "[12]" [ref=e512] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-23"
            - text: However, continuous cropping after 3–4 years decrease grain yields significantly.
            - superscript [ref=e513]:

          - paragraph [ref=e519]:
            - text: A common pest of grain legumes that is noticed in the tropical and subtropical Asia, Africa, Australia and Oceania are minuscule flies that belong to the family
            - link "Agromyzidae" [ref=e521] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Agromyzidae
            - text: ", dubbed \"bean flies\". They are considered to be the most destructive. The host range of these flies is very wide amongst cultivated legumes. Infestation of plants starts from germination through to harvest, and they can destroy an entire crop in early stage."
            - superscript [ref=e522]:
              - link "[14]" [ref=e523] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-25"
            - link "Black bean aphids" [ref=e524] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Black_bean_aphid
            - text: are a serious pest to broad beans and other beans. Common hosts for this pest are fathen, thistle and dock.
            - link "Pea weevil" [ref=e525] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Pea_weevil
            - text: and
            - link "bean weevil" [ref=e526] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Bean_weevil
            - text: damage leaf margins leaving characteristics semi-circular notches.
            - link "Stem nematodes" [ref=e527] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Stem_nematode
            - text: are very widespread but will be found more frequently in areas where host plants are grown.

          - paragraph [ref=e567]:
            - text: Seed viability decreases with longer storage time. Studies of
            - link "vetch" [ref=e568] [cursor=pointer]:

            - text: ","

            - text: ", and peas show that they last about 5 years in storage. Environmental factors that are important in influencing germination are relative humidity and temperature.           - paragraph [ref=e608]:
            - text: Legumes are a key ingredient in vegan meat and dairy

            - text: . They are growing in use as a plant-based protein source in the world marketplace.

            - text: Products containing legumes grew by 39% in Europe between 2013 and 2017.

          - paragraph [ref=e616]:
            - text: There is a
            - link "common misconception" [ref=e617] [cursor=pointer]:

            - text: that adding salt before cooking prevents them from cooking through. Legumes may not soften because they are old, or because of
            - link "hard water" [ref=e618] [cursor=pointer]:

            - text: or
            - link "acidic" [ref=e619] [cursor=pointer]:

            - link "seasoning" [ref=e620] [cursor=pointer]:

          - paragraph [ref=e629]:
            - text: Legumes are a significant source of
            - link "protein" [ref=e630] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Protein_(nutrient)
            - text: ","
            - link "dietary fibre" [ref=e631] [cursor=pointer]:

            - text: ","
            - link "carbohydrates" [ref=e632] [cursor=pointer]:

            - text: ", and"
            - link "dietary minerals" [ref=e633] [cursor=pointer]:

            - text: ; for example, a 100-gram serving of cooked
            - link "chickpeas" [ref=e634] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Chickpea
            - text: contains 18 percent of the
            - link "Daily Value" [ref=e635] [cursor=pointer]:

            - text: (DV) for protein, 30 percent DV for dietary fiber, 43 percent DV for
            - link "folate" [ref=e636] [cursor=pointer]:

            - text: and 52 percent DV for
            - link "manganese" [ref=e637] [cursor=pointer]:

          - paragraph [ref=e640]:
            - text: Legumes are an excellent source of
            - link "resistant starch" [ref=e641] [cursor=pointer]:

            - link "butyrate" [ref=e645] [cursor=pointer]:

            - link "food energy" [ref=e646] [cursor=pointer]:

            - text: ","
            - link "clover" [ref=e660] [cursor=pointer]:

            - link "Stylosanthes" [ref=e664] [cursor=pointer]:

            - text: ), or
            - link "Arachis" [ref=e666] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Arachis
            - text: ", are sown in"
            - link "pasture" [ref=e667] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Pasture
            - text: and grazed by livestock. Others, such as
            - link "Leucaena" [ref=e669] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Leucaena
            - text: or
            - link "Albizia" [ref=e671] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Albizia
            - text: ", are woody shrubs or trees that are either broken down by livestock or regularly cut by humans to provide fodder. Legume-based feeds improve animal performance over a diet of perennial grasses. Factors include larger consumption, faster digestion, and higher"
            - link "feed conversion rate" [ref=e672] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Feed_conversion_rate
            - text: .
            - superscript [ref=e673]:

          - paragraph [ref=e675]:

            - link "Gliricidia sepium" [ref=e677] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Gliricidia_sepium
            - text: can be planted along edges of fields to provide shade for cattle, the leaves and bark are often eaten by cattle. Green manure can be grown between harvesting the main crop and the planting of the next crop.

          - paragraph [ref=e689]:
            - text: Legume species grown for their flowers include
            - link "lupins" [ref=e690] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Lupin
            - text: ", which are farmed commercially for their blooms as well as being popular in gardens worldwide. Industrially farmed legumes include"

            - text: and
            - link "Acacia" [ref=e694] [cursor=pointer]:

            - text: species, which are cultivated for
            - link "dye" [ref=e695] [cursor=pointer]:

            - text: and
            - link "natural gum" [ref=e696] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Natural_gum
            - text: production, respectively.
            - link "Fallow" [ref=e697] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Fallow
            - text: or
            - link "green manure" [ref=e698] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Green_manure
            - text: legume species are cultivated to be tilled back into the soil in order to exploit the high levels of captured atmospheric nitrogen found in the roots of most legumes. Numerous legumes farmed for this purpose include
            - link "Leucaena" [ref=e700] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Leucaena
            - text: ","
            - link "Cyamopsis" [ref=e702] [cursor=pointer]:

            - text: ", and"
            - link "Sesbania" [ref=e704] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Sesbania
            - text: species. Various legume species are farmed for timber production worldwide, including numerous
            - link "Acacia" [ref=e706] [cursor=pointer]:

            - text: species and
            - link "Castanospermum australe" [ref=e708] [cursor=pointer]:

              - link "[35]" [ref=e750] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-Albala2007-46"
            - text: Dry pea seeds have been discovered in a Swiss village that are believed to date back to the
            - link "Stone Age" [ref=e751] [cursor=pointer]:

            - link "Mesopotamian" [ref=e752] [cursor=pointer]:

            - superscript [ref=e753]:

            - text: The soybean was domesticated around 5,000 years ago in China from a descendant of the wild vine Glycine soja.

            - text: Genetic analyses of the common bean Phaseolus show that it originated in

            - link "maize" [ref=e763] [cursor=pointer]:

            - text: The

            - text: Many legumes contain

            - text: are one exception to this rule). These bacteria have the special ability of

          - paragraph [ref=e480]:
            - text: This arrangement means that the root nodules are sources of nitrogen for legumes, making them relatively rich in nitrogenous

            - text: and

            - text: . Nitrogen is therefore a necessary
            - link "ingredient" [ref=e483] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Ingredient
            - text: in the production of proteins.
          - paragraph [ref=e484]:
            - text: When a legume plant dies in the field, for example following the
            - link "harvest" [ref=e485] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Harvest
            - text: ", all of its remaining nitrogen, incorporated into"
            - link "amino acids" [ref=e486] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Amino_acid
            - text: inside the remaining plant parts, is released back into the soil. In the soil, the amino acids are converted to nitrate (
            - generic [ref=e487]:
              - text: "NO"
              - generic [ref=e488]:
                - generic [ref=e489]: −
                - generic [ref=e490]: "3"
            - text: ), making the nitrogen available to other plants, thereby serving as fertilizer for future crops.
            - superscript [ref=e491]:

            - superscript [ref=e493]:

            - text: In many traditional and

            - text: involving legumes is common. By alternating between legumes and non-legumes, or by growing both together for part of the growing season, the field can receive a sufficient amount of nitrogenous compounds to produce a good result without adding nitrogenous fertilizer. Legumes are often used as
            - link "green manure" [ref=e504] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Green_manure

              - text: "]"
          - paragraph [ref=e508]:
            - text: Sri Lanka developed the
            - link "polyculture" [ref=e509] [cursor=pointer]:

            - text: practice known as coconut-soybean
            - link "intercropping" [ref=e510] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Intercropping
            - text: ". Grain legumes are grown in coconut (Cocos nuficera) groves in two ways: intercropping or as a cash crop. These are grown mainly for their protein, vegetable oil and ability to uphold soil fertility."
            - superscript [ref=e511]:
              - link "[12]" [ref=e512] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-23"
            - text: However, continuous cropping after 3–4 years decrease grain yields significantly.

            - text: ", dubbed \"bean flies\". They are considered to be the most destructive. The host range of these flies is very wide amongst cultivated legumes. Infestation of plants starts from germination through to harvest, and they can destroy an entire crop in early stage."
            - superscript [ref=e522]:
              - link "[14]" [ref=e523] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-25"
            - link "Black bean aphids" [ref=e524] [cursor=pointer]:

            - superscript [ref=e558]:
              - link "[16]" [ref=e559] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-27"
          - paragraph [ref=e560]:
            - text: Abiotic problems include nutrient deficiencies, (nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium, copper, magnesium, manganese, boron, zinc), pollutants (air, water, soil, pesticide injury, fertilizer burn), toxic concentration of minerals, and unfavorable growth conditions.
            - superscript [ref=e561]:
              - link "[17]" [ref=e562] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-28"
          - generic [ref=e563]:
            - heading "Storage" [level=2] [ref=e564]
            - generic [ref=e565]:
              - text: "["
              - link "edit" [ref=e566] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /w/index.php?title=Legume&action=edit&section=6
              - text: "]"
          - paragraph [ref=e567]:
            - text: Seed viability decreases with longer storage time. Studies of
            - link "vetch" [ref=e568] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Vetch
            - text: ","
            - link "broad beans" [ref=e569] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Broad_bean
            - text: ", and peas show that they last about 5 years in storage. Environmental factors that are important in influencing germination are relative humidity and temperature. Two rules apply to moisture content between 5 and 14 percent: the life of the seed will last longer if the storage temperature is reduced by 5 degree Celsius. Secondly, the storage moisture content will decrease if temperature is reduced by 1 degree Celsius."
            - superscript [ref=e570]:
              - link "[18]" [ref=e571] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-29"
          - generic [ref=e572]:
            - heading "Uses" [level=2] [ref=e573]
            - generic [ref=e574]:
              - text: "["
              - link "edit" [ref=e575] [cursor=pointer]:

              - text: "]"
          - figure "Pulses in a Nanglo tray" [ref=e576]:

            - generic [ref=e579]:
              - text: Pulses in a
              - link "Nanglo" [ref=e580] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Nanglo
              - text: tray
          - paragraph [ref=e581]:
            - text: Cultivated legumes encompass a diverse range of
            - link "agricultural" [ref=e582] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Agriculture
            - text: classifications, spanning
            - link "forage" [ref=e583] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Forage
            - text: ","
            - link "grain" [ref=e584] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Grain
            - text: ", flowering, pharmaceutical/industrial, fallow/green manure, and timber categories. A notable characteristic of many commercially cultivated legume species is their versatility, often assuming multiple roles concurrently. The extent of these roles is contingent upon the stage of maturity at which they are harvested."
            - superscript [ref=e585]:
              - text: "["
              - link "citation needed" [ref=e587] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed

              - link "indehiscent" [ref=e597] [cursor=pointer]:

          - paragraph [ref=e598]:
            - text: Grain legumes are cultivated for their seeds,
            - superscript [ref=e599]:
              - link "[19]" [ref=e600] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-crops-30"
            - text: for humans and animals to eat, or for oils for industrial uses. Grain legumes include
            - link "beans" [ref=e601] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Bean
            - text: ","
            - link "lentils" [ref=e602] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Lentil
            - text: ","
            - link "lupins" [ref=e603] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Lupin
            - text: ","
            - link "peas" [ref=e604] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Pea
            - text: ", and"
            - link "peanuts" [ref=e605] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Peanut
            - text: .
            - superscript [ref=e606]:
              - link "[20]" [ref=e607] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-31"
          - paragraph [ref=e608]:
            - text: Legumes are a key ingredient in vegan meat and dairy
            - link "substitutes" [ref=e609] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Meat_analogue
            - text: . They are growing in use as a plant-based protein source in the world marketplace.
            - superscript [ref=e610]:
              - link "[21]" [ref=e611] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-sc-australian-32"
            - superscript [ref=e612]:
              - link "[22]" [ref=e613] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-33"
            - text: Products containing legumes grew by 39% in Europe between 2013 and 2017.
            - superscript [ref=e614]:
              - link "[23]" [ref=e615] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-eu-growth-34"
          - paragraph [ref=e616]:
            - text: There is a
            - link "common misconception" [ref=e617] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/List_of_common_misconceptions
            - text: that adding salt before cooking prevents them from cooking through. Legumes may not soften because they are old, or because of
            - link "hard water" [ref=e618] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Hard_water
            - text: or
            - link "acidic" [ref=e619] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Acid
            - text: ingredients in the pot; salting before cooking results in better
            - link "seasoning" [ref=e620] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Seasoning
            - text: .
            - superscript [ref=e621]:
              - link "[24]" [ref=e622] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-35"
            - superscript [ref=e623]:
              - link "[25]" [ref=e624] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-36"
          - generic [ref=e625]:
            - heading "Nutritional value" [level=4] [ref=e626]
            - generic [ref=e627]:
              - text: "["
              - link "edit" [ref=e628] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /w/index.php?title=Legume&action=edit&section=9
              - text: "]"
          - paragraph [ref=e629]:
            - text: Legumes are a significant source of
            - link "protein" [ref=e630] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Protein_(nutrient)
            - text: ","
            - link "dietary fibre" [ref=e631] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Dietary_fiber
            - text: ","
            - link "carbohydrates" [ref=e632] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Carbohydrate
            - text: ", and"
            - link "dietary minerals" [ref=e633] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Dietary_minerals
            - text: ; for example, a 100-gram serving of cooked
            - link "chickpeas" [ref=e634] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Chickpea
            - text: contains 18 percent of the
            - link "Daily Value" [ref=e635] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Daily_Value
            - text: (DV) for protein, 30 percent DV for dietary fiber, 43 percent DV for
            - link "folate" [ref=e636] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Folate
            - text: and 52 percent DV for
            - link "manganese" [ref=e637] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Manganese
            - text: .
            - superscript [ref=e638]:
              - link "[26]" [ref=e639] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-nd-37"
          - paragraph [ref=e640]:
            - text: Legumes are an excellent source of
            - link "resistant starch" [ref=e641] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Resistant_starch
            - text: ; this is broken down by
            - link "bacteria" [ref=e642] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Gut_flora
            - text: in the
            - link "large intestine" [ref=e643] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Large_intestine
            - text: to produce
            - link "short-chain fatty acids" [ref=e644] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Short-chain_fatty_acid
            - text: (such as
            - link "butyrate" [ref=e645] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Butyrate
            - text: ) used by intestinal cells for
            - link "food energy" [ref=e646] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Food_energy
            - text: .
            - superscript [ref=e647]:
              - link "[27]" [ref=e648] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-38"
          - generic [ref=e649]:

          - figure "White clover, a forage crop" [ref=e653]:

            - generic [ref=e656]:
              - text: White
              - link "clover" [ref=e657] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Clover
              - text: ", a forage crop"
          - paragraph [ref=e658]:
            - text: Forage legumes are of two broad types. Some, like
            - link "alfalfa" [ref=e659] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Alfalfa
            - text: ","
            - link "clover" [ref=e660] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Clover
            - text: ", vetch ("
            - link "Vicia" [ref=e662] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Vicia
            - text: ), stylo (
            - link "Stylosanthes" [ref=e664] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Stylosanthes
            - text: ), or
            - link "Arachis" [ref=e666] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Arachis
            - text: ", are sown in"
            - link "pasture" [ref=e667] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Pasture
            - text: and grazed by livestock. Others, such as
            - link "Leucaena" [ref=e669] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Leucaena
            - text: or
            - link "Albizia" [ref=e671] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Albizia
            - text: ", are woody shrubs or trees that are either broken down by livestock or regularly cut by humans to provide fodder. Legume-based feeds improve animal performance over a diet of perennial grasses. Factors include larger consumption, faster digestion, and higher"
            - link "feed conversion rate" [ref=e672] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Feed_conversion_rate
            - text: .
            - superscript [ref=e673]:
              - link "[28]" [ref=e674] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-39"
          - paragraph [ref=e675]:
            - text: The type of crop grown for animal rearing depends on the farming system. In cattle rearing, legume trees such as
            - link "Gliricidia sepium" [ref=e677] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Gliricidia_sepium
            - text: can be planted along edges of fields to provide shade for cattle, the leaves and bark are often eaten by cattle. Green manure can be grown between harvesting the main crop and the planting of the next crop.
            - superscript [ref=e678]:
              - link "[29]" [ref=e679] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-40"
          - generic [ref=e680]:
            - heading "Other uses" [level=3] [ref=e681]

              - text: "["
              - link "edit" [ref=e683] [cursor=pointer]:

              - text: "]"
          - figure "Lupin flower garden" [ref=e684]:

              - /url: /wiki/File:Flower_garden_in_Ushuaia_(5542996965).jpg
              - img [ref=e686]
            - generic [ref=e687]:
              - link "Lupin" [ref=e688] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Lupin
              - text: flower garden
          - paragraph [ref=e689]:
            - text: Legume species grown for their flowers include
            - link "lupins" [ref=e690] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Lupin
            - text: ", which are farmed commercially for their blooms as well as being popular in gardens worldwide. Industrially farmed legumes include"
            - link "Indigofera" [ref=e692] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Indigofera
            - text: and
            - link "Acacia" [ref=e694] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Acacia
            - text: species, which are cultivated for
            - link "dye" [ref=e695] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Dye
            - text: and
            - link "natural gum" [ref=e696] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Natural_gum
            - text: production, respectively.
            - link "Fallow" [ref=e697] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Fallow
            - text: or
            - link "green manure" [ref=e698] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Green_manure
            - text: legume species are cultivated to be tilled back into the soil in order to exploit the high levels of captured atmospheric nitrogen found in the roots of most legumes. Numerous legumes farmed for this purpose include
            - link "Leucaena" [ref=e700] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Leucaena
            - text: ","
            - link "Cyamopsis" [ref=e702] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Cyamopsis
            - text: ", and"
            - link "Sesbania" [ref=e704] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Sesbania
            - text: species. Various legume species are farmed for timber production worldwide, including numerous
            - link "Acacia" [ref=e706] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Acacia
            - text: species and
            - link "Castanospermum australe" [ref=e708] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Castanospermum_australe
            - text: .
            - superscript [ref=e709]:
              - text: "["
              - link "citation needed" [ref=e711] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed
              - text: "]"
          - paragraph [ref=e712]:
            - text: Some legume trees, like the
            - link "honey locust" [ref=e713] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Honey_locust
            - text: (
            - link "Gleditsia" [ref=e715] [cursor=pointer]:

            - text: .

            - text: Others, including the black locust (
            - link "Robinia pseudoacacia" [ref=e720] [cursor=pointer]:

            - link "Gymnocladus dioicus" [ref=e724] [cursor=pointer]:

            - text: ),
            - superscript [ref=e725]:

              - link "[35]" [ref=e750] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-Albala2007-46"
            - text: Dry pea seeds have been discovered in a Swiss village that are believed to date back to the
            - link "Stone Age" [ref=e751] [cursor=pointer]:

            - link "Mesopotamian" [ref=e752] [cursor=pointer]:

            - superscript [ref=e753]:

                - /url: "#cite_note-b1-47"
            - text: The soybean was domesticated around 5,000 years ago in China from a descendant of the wild vine Glycine soja.

            - text: The oldest-known domesticated beans in the Americas were found in

            - superscript [ref=e760]:

            - text: Genetic analyses of the common bean Phaseolus show that it originated in

            - link "maize" [ref=e763] [cursor=pointer]:

You are the WebSurfer agent. You retrieve information from the web by navigating and interacting with pages, exactly as a human would.

## Navigation policy
- Unless the user explicitly provides a URL or names a specific website to visit, always start at google.com. Open Google, type your search query, read the results, and follow links by clicking — do not jump directly to any URL, and do not construct or guess URLs from memory or training data.

## Page size management (critical)
Loading large, unfiltered pages makes it hard to locate relevant information and risks exceeding LLM context length limits. Before loading any page, actively try to reduce its size:
- Use the site's search box with specific keywords rather than browsing index pages.
- Apply any available filters: date range, category, author, language, file type, etc.
- Prefer paginated or scoped views over full listing pages.

## Tool selection
- Prefer specialized tools (ArXiv, Wikipedia, YouTube, direct download, etc.) when they directly match the task. Use browser automation only when no dedicated tool fits.
- Only Google Search is permitted as a search engine.
- For academic paper searches, prefer Google Scholar, arXiv, and DBLP.

## Output
- Produce well-structured, detailed output as required. Extract only what is relevant to the task.
- If you use browser tools to save any content, the browser will store it under the directory: [<PROJECT_ROOT>/tmp/browser_wp]. This is enforced by the browser itself — you only need to report the file path in your output when needed.

Work carefully, efficiently, and stay within your assigned retrieval scope.

                  - text: The

                  - link "Wars of the Roses" [ref=e114] [cursor=pointer]:

                  - link "King Henry VI" [ref=e115] [cursor=pointer]:

                  - text: to St Paul's, with adversaries walking together, holding hands. Contemporaries varied in their views of the accord. Some wrote verses expressing hope that it would lead to new-found peace and prosperity; others were more pessimistic. In the long run, the King's Loveday and its agreements had no long-lasting benefit. Within a few months, petty violence between the lords had broken out again.           - paragraph [ref=e480]:
            - text: This arrangement means that the root nodules are sources of nitrogen for legumes, making them relatively rich in nitrogenous

          - paragraph [ref=e484]:
            - text: When a legume plant dies in the field, for example following the

            - text: ", all of its remaining nitrogen, incorporated into"
            - link "amino acids" [ref=e486] [cursor=pointer]:

            - generic [ref=e487]:

              - generic [ref=e488]:

            - text: In many traditional and

By alternating between legumes and non-legumes, or by growing both together for part of the growing season, the field can receive a sufficient amount of nitrogenous compounds to produce a good result without adding nitrogenous fertilizer. Legumes are often used as

          - paragraph [ref=e508]:
            - text: Sri Lanka developed the
            - link "polyculture" [ref=e509] [cursor=pointer]:

            - text: practice known as coconut-soybean
            - link "intercropping" [ref=e510] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Intercropping
            - text: ". Grain legumes are grown in coconut (Cocos nuficera) groves in two ways: intercropping or as a cash crop. These are grown mainly for their protein, vegetable oil and ability to uphold soil fertility."

              - link "[12]" [ref=e512] [cursor=pointer]:

          - paragraph [ref=e519]:

            - link "Agromyzidae" [ref=e521] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Agromyzidae
            - text: ", dubbed \"bean flies\". They are considered to be the most destructive. The host range of these flies is very wide amongst cultivated legumes. Infestation of plants starts from germination through to harvest, and they can destroy an entire crop in early stage."
            - superscript [ref=e522]:

                - /url: "#cite_note-25"
            - link "Black bean aphids" [ref=e524] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Black_bean_aphid
            - text: are a serious pest to broad beans and other beans. Common hosts for this pest are fathen, thistle and dock.

            - text: and

          - paragraph [ref=e567]:

              - text: ", a forage crop"
          - paragraph [ref=e658]:
            - text: Forage legumes are of two broad types. Some, like
            - link "alfalfa" [ref=e659] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Alfalfa
            - text: ","
            - link "clover" [ref=e660] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Clover
            - text: ", vetch ("
            - link "Vicia" [ref=e662] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Vicia
            - text: ), stylo (
            - link "Stylosanthes" [ref=e664] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Stylosanthes
            - text: ), or
            - link "Arachis" [ref=e666] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Arachis
            - text: ", are sown in"
            - link "pasture" [ref=e667] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Pasture
            - text: and grazed by livestock. Others, such as
            - link "Leucaena" [ref=e669] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Leucaena
            - text: or
            - link "Albizia" [ref=e671] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Albizia
            - text: ", are woody shrubs or trees that are either broken down by livestock or regularly cut by humans to provide fodder. Legume-based feeds improve animal performance over a diet of perennial grasses. Factors include larger consumption, faster digestion, and higher"
            - link "feed conversion rate" [ref=e672] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Feed_conversion_rate
            - text: .
            - superscript [ref=e673]:
              - link "[28]" [ref=e674] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-39"
          - paragraph [ref=e675]:
            - text: The type of crop grown for animal rearing depends on the farming system. In cattle rearing, legume trees such as
            - link "Gliricidia sepium" [ref=e677] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Gliricidia_sepium
            - text: can be planted along edges of fields to provide shade for cattle, the leaves and bark are often eaten by cattle. Green manure can be grown between harvesting the main crop and the planting of the next crop.
            - superscript [ref=e678]:
              - link "[29]" [ref=e679] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-40"
          - generic [ref=e680]:
            - heading "Other uses" [level=3] [ref=e681]
            - generic [ref=e682]:
              - text: "["
              - link "edit" [ref=e683] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /w/index.php?title=Legume&action=edit&section=11
              - text: "]"
          - figure "Lupin flower garden" [ref=e684]:
            - link [ref=e685] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/File:Flower_garden_in_Ushuaia_(5542996965).jpg
              - img [ref=e686]
            - generic [ref=e687]:
              - link "Lupin" [ref=e688] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Lupin
              - text: flower garden
          - paragraph [ref=e689]:
            - text: Legume species grown for their flowers include
            - link "lupins" [ref=e690] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Lupin
            - text: ", which are farmed commercially for their blooms as well as being popular in gardens worldwide. Industrially farmed legumes include"
            - link "Indigofera" [ref=e692] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Indigofera
            - text: and
            - link "Acacia" [ref=e694] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Acacia
            - text: species, which are cultivated for
            - link "dye" [ref=e695] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Dye
            - text: and
            - link "natural gum" [ref=e696] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Natural_gum
            - text: production, respectively.
            - link "Fallow" [ref=e697] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Fallow
            - text: or
            - link "green manure" [ref=e698] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Green_manure
            - text: legume species are cultivated to be tilled back into the soil in order to exploit the high levels of captured atmospheric nitrogen found in the roots of most legumes. Numerous legumes farmed for this purpose include
            - link "Leucaena" [ref=e700] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Leucaena
            - text: ","
            - link "Cyamopsis" [ref=e702] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Cyamopsis
            - text: ", and"
            - link "Sesbania" [ref=e704] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Sesbania
            - text: species. Various legume species are farmed for timber production worldwide, including numerous
            - link "Acacia" [ref=e706] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Acacia
            - text: species and
            - link "Castanospermum australe" [ref=e708] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Castanospermum_australe
            - text: .
            - superscript [ref=e709]:
              - text: "["
              - link "citation needed" [ref=e711] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed
              - text: "]"
          - paragraph [ref=e712]:
            - text: Some legume trees, like the
            - link "honey locust" [ref=e713] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Honey_locust
            - text: (
            - link "Gleditsia" [ref=e715] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Gleditsia
            - text: ) can be used in
            - link "agroforestry" [ref=e716] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Agroforestry
            - text: .
            - superscript [ref=e717]:
              - link "[30]" [ref=e718] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-41"
            - text: Others, including the black locust (
            - link "Robinia pseudoacacia" [ref=e720] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Robinia_pseudoacacia
            - text: ),
            - superscript [ref=e721]:
              - link "[31]" [ref=e722] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-42"
            - text: Kentucky coffeetree (
            - link "Gymnocladus dioicus" [ref=e724] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Kentucky_coffeetree
            - text: ),
            - superscript [ref=e725]:
              - link "[32]" [ref=e726] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-43"
            - generic [ref=e727]:
              - link "Laburnum" [ref=e728] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Laburnum
              - text: ","
            - superscript [ref=e729]:
              - link "[33]" [ref=e730] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-44"
            - text: and the woody climbing vine
            - link "Wisteria" [ref=e732] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Wisteria
            - text: ", have"
            - link "poisonous" [ref=e733] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Poison
            - text: elements.
          - generic [ref=e734]:
            - heading "History" [level=2] [ref=e735]
            - generic [ref=e736]:
              - text: "["
              - link "edit" [ref=e737] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /w/index.php?title=Legume&action=edit&section=12
              - text: "]"
          - paragraph [ref=e738]:
            - link "Neanderthals" [ref=e739] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Neanderthal
            - text: and
            - link "early modern humans" [ref=e740] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Early_modern_humans
            - text: used wild pulses when cooking meals 70,000 to 40,000 years ago.
            - superscript [ref=e741]:
              - link "[34]" [ref=e742] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-45"
            - text: Traces of pulse production have been found around the
            - link "Ravi River" [ref=e743] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Ravi_River
            - text: (
            - link "Punjab" [ref=e744] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Punjab_(region)
            - text: ), the seat of the
            - link "Indus Valley civilisation" [ref=e745] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Indus_Valley_civilisation
            - text: ", from c. 3300 BC. Meanwhile, evidence of lentil cultivation has also been found in Egyptian"
            - link "pyramids" [ref=e746] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Pyramid
            - text: and
            - link "cuneiform" [ref=e747] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Cuneiform
            - link "recipes" [ref=e748] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Recipe
            - text: .
            - superscript [ref=e749]:
              - link "[35]" [ref=e750] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-Albala2007-46"
            - text: Dry pea seeds have been discovered in a Swiss village that are believed to date back to the
            - link "Stone Age" [ref=e751] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Stone_Age
            - text: . Archaeological evidence suggests that these peas must have been grown in the eastern Mediterranean and
            - link "Mesopotamian" [ref=e752] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Mesopotamia
            - text: regions at least 5,000 years ago and in Britain as early as the 11th century.
            - superscript [ref=e753]:
              - link "[36]" [ref=e754] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-b1-47"
            - text: The soybean was domesticated around 5,000 years ago in China from a descendant of the wild vine Glycine soja.
            - superscript [ref=e755]:
              - link "[37]" [ref=e756] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-48"
          - paragraph [ref=e757]:
            - text: The oldest-known domesticated beans in the Americas were found in
            - link "Guitarrero Cave" [ref=e758] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Guitarrero_Cave
            - text: ", an archaeological site in"
            - link "Peru" [ref=e759] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Peru
            - text: ", and dated to around the second millennium BCE."
            - superscript [ref=e760]:
              - link "[38]" [ref=e761] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-Chazan-49"
            - text: Genetic analyses of the common bean Phaseolus show that it originated in
            - link "Mesoamerica" [ref=e762] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Mesoamerica
            - text: ", and subsequently spread southward, along with"
            - link "maize" [ref=e763] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Maize
            - text: and squash, traditional companion crops.
            - superscript [ref=e764]:
              - link "[39]" [ref=e765] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-50"
            - text: In the United States, the domesticated soybean was introduced in 1770 by
            - link "Benjamin Franklin" [ref=e766] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Benjamin_Franklin
            - text: after he sent seeds to Philadelphia from France.
            - superscript [ref=e767]:
              - link "[40]" [ref=e768] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-51"

            - link [ref=e776] [cursor=pointer]:

          - paragraph [ref=e780]:
            - text: The International Year of Pulses 2016 was declared by the
            - link "Sixty-eighth session of the United Nations General Assembly" [ref=e781] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Sixty-eighth_session_of_the_United_Nations_General_Assembly
            - text: .
            - superscript [ref=e782]:
              - link "[41]" [ref=e783] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-iyp-52"
            - text: The
            - link "Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations" [ref=e784] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Food_and_Agriculture_Organization_of_the_United_Nations
            - text: was nominated to facilitate the implementation of the year in collaboration with governments, relevant organizations, non-governmental organizations and other relevant stakeholders. Its aim was to heighten public awareness of the nutritional benefits of pulses as part of
            - link "sustainable food" [ref=e785] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Sustainable_food_systems
            - text: production aimed towards
            - link "food security" [ref=e786] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Food_security
            - text: and
            - link "nutrition" [ref=e787] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Nutrition
            - text: . The year created an opportunity to encourage connections throughout the food chain that would better use pulse-based proteins, further global production of pulses, better use
            - link "crop rotations" [ref=e788] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Crop_rotation
            - text: and address challenges in the global trade of pulses.
            - superscript [ref=e789]:
              - link "[41]" [ref=e790] [cursor=pointer]:

You are the WebSurfer agent. You retrieve information from the web by navigating and interacting with pages, exactly as a human would.

## Navigation policy
- Unless the user explicitly provides a URL or names a specific website to visit, always start at google.com. Open Google, type your search query, read the results, and follow links by clicking — do not jump directly to any URL, and do not construct or guess URLs from memory or training data.

## Page size management (critical)
Loading large, unfiltered pages makes it hard to locate relevant information and risks exceeding LLM context length limits. Before loading any page, actively try to reduce its size:
- Use the site's search box with specific keywords rather than browsing index pages.
- Apply any available filters: date range, category, author, language, file type, etc.
- Prefer paginated or scoped views over full listing pages.

## Tool selection
- Prefer specialized tools (ArXiv, Wikipedia, YouTube, direct download, etc.) when they directly match the task. Use browser automation only when no dedicated tool fits.
- Only Google Search is permitted as a search engine.
- For academic paper searches, prefer Google Scholar, arXiv, and DBLP.

## Output
- Produce well-structured, detailed output as required. Extract only what is relevant to the task.
- If you use browser tools to save any content, the browser will store it under the directory: [<PROJECT_ROOT>/tmp/browser_wp]. This is enforced by the browser itself — you only need to report the file path in your output when needed.

Work carefully, efficiently, and stay within your assigned retrieval scope.

          - paragraph [ref=e480]:
            - text: This arrangement means that the root nodules are sources of nitrogen for legumes, making them relatively rich in nitrogenous

          - paragraph [ref=e484]:
            - text: When a legume plant dies in the field, for example following the
            - link "harvest" [ref=e485] [cursor=pointer]:

            - text: ", all of its remaining nitrogen, incorporated into"

            - text: In many traditional and

By alternating between legumes and non-legumes, or by growing both together for part of the growing season, the field can receive a sufficient amount of nitrogenous compounds to produce a good result without adding nitrogenous fertilizer. Legumes are often used as
            - link "green manure" [ref=e504] [cursor=pointer]:

          - paragraph [ref=e508]:
            - text: Sri Lanka developed the
            - link "polyculture" [ref=e509] [cursor=pointer]:

            - text: practice known as coconut-soybean
            - link "intercropping" [ref=e510] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Intercropping
            - text: ". Grain legumes are grown in coconut (Cocos nuficera) groves in two ways: intercropping or as a cash crop. These are grown mainly for their protein, vegetable oil and ability to uphold soil fertility."
            - superscript [ref=e511]:
              - link "[12]" [ref=e512] [cursor=pointer]:

              - /url: /wiki/Agromyzidae
            - text: ", dubbed \"bean flies\". They are considered to be the most destructive. The host range of these flies is very wide amongst cultivated legumes. Infestation of plants starts from germination through to harvest, and they can destroy an entire crop in early stage."
            - superscript [ref=e522]:
              - link "[14]" [ref=e523] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-25"
            - link "Black bean aphids" [ref=e524] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Black_bean_aphid
            - text: are a serious pest to broad beans and other beans. Common hosts for this pest are fathen, thistle and dock.

            - text: and
            - link "bean weevil" [ref=e526] [cursor=pointer]:

          - paragraph [ref=e567]:
            - text: Seed viability decreases with longer storage time. Studies of

            - text: ","

              - text: "["
              - link "edit" [ref=e628] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /w/index.php?title=Legume&action=edit&section=9
              - text: "]"
          - paragraph [ref=e629]:
            - text: Legumes are a significant source of
            - link "protein" [ref=e630] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Protein_(nutrient)
            - text: ","
            - link "dietary fibre" [ref=e631] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Dietary_fiber
            - text: ","
            - link "carbohydrates" [ref=e632] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Carbohydrate
            - text: ", and"
            - link "dietary minerals" [ref=e633] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Dietary_minerals
            - text: ; for example, a 100-gram serving of cooked
            - link "chickpeas" [ref=e634] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Chickpea
            - text: contains 18 percent of the
            - link "Daily Value" [ref=e635] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Daily_Value
            - text: (DV) for protein, 30 percent DV for dietary fiber, 43 percent DV for
            - link "folate" [ref=e636] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Folate
            - text: and 52 percent DV for
            - link "manganese" [ref=e637] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Manganese
            - text: .
            - superscript [ref=e638]:
              - link "[26]" [ref=e639] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-nd-37"
          - paragraph [ref=e640]:
            - text: Legumes are an excellent source of
            - link "resistant starch" [ref=e641] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Resistant_starch
            - text: ; this is broken down by
            - link "bacteria" [ref=e642] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Gut_flora
            - text: in the
            - link "large intestine" [ref=e643] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Large_intestine
            - text: to produce
            - link "short-chain fatty acids" [ref=e644] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Short-chain_fatty_acid
            - text: (such as
            - link "butyrate" [ref=e645] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Butyrate
            - text: ) used by intestinal cells for
            - link "food energy" [ref=e646] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Food_energy
            - text: .
            - superscript [ref=e647]:
              - link "[27]" [ref=e648] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-38"
          - generic [ref=e649]:
            - heading "Forage" [level=3] [ref=e650]
            - generic [ref=e651]:
              - text: "["
              - link "edit" [ref=e652] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /w/index.php?title=Legume&action=edit&section=10
              - text: "]"
          - figure "White clover, a forage crop" [ref=e653]:
            - link [ref=e654] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/File:TrifoliumRepensFlowers.jpg
              - img [ref=e655]
            - generic [ref=e656]:
              - text: White
              - link "clover" [ref=e657] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Clover
              - text: ", a forage crop"
          - paragraph [ref=e658]:
            - text: Forage legumes are of two broad types. Some, like
            - link "alfalfa" [ref=e659] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Alfalfa
            - text: ","
            - link "clover" [ref=e660] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Clover
            - text: ", vetch ("
            - link "Vicia" [ref=e662] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Vicia
            - text: ), stylo (
            - link "Stylosanthes" [ref=e664] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Stylosanthes
            - text: ), or
            - link "Arachis" [ref=e666] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Arachis
            - text: ", are sown in"
            - link "pasture" [ref=e667] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Pasture
            - text: and grazed by livestock. Others, such as
            - link "Leucaena" [ref=e669] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Leucaena
            - text: or
            - link "Albizia" [ref=e671] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Albizia
            - text: ", are woody shrubs or trees that are either broken down by livestock or regularly cut by humans to provide fodder. Legume-based feeds improve animal performance over a diet of perennial grasses. Factors include larger consumption, faster digestion, and higher"
            - link "feed conversion rate" [ref=e672] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Feed_conversion_rate
            - text: .
            - superscript [ref=e673]:
              - link "[28]" [ref=e674] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-39"
          - paragraph [ref=e675]:
            - text: The type of crop grown for animal rearing depends on the farming system. In cattle rearing, legume trees such as
            - link "Gliricidia sepium" [ref=e677] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Gliricidia_sepium
            - text: can be planted along edges of fields to provide shade for cattle, the leaves and bark are often eaten by cattle. Green manure can be grown between harvesting the main crop and the planting of the next crop.
            - superscript [ref=e678]:
              - link "[29]" [ref=e679] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-40"
          - generic [ref=e680]:
            - heading "Other uses" [level=3] [ref=e681]
            - generic [ref=e682]:
              - text: "["
              - link "edit" [ref=e683] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /w/index.php?title=Legume&action=edit&section=11
              - text: "]"
          - figure "Lupin flower garden" [ref=e684]:
            - link [ref=e685] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/File:Flower_garden_in_Ushuaia_(5542996965).jpg
              - img [ref=e686]
            - generic [ref=e687]:
              - link "Lupin" [ref=e688] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Lupin
              - text: flower garden
          - paragraph [ref=e689]:
            - text: Legume species grown for their flowers include
            - link "lupins" [ref=e690] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Lupin
            - text: ", which are farmed commercially for their blooms as well as being popular in gardens worldwide. Industrially farmed legumes include"
            - link "Indigofera" [ref=e692] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Indigofera
            - text: and
            - link "Acacia" [ref=e694] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Acacia
            - text: species, which are cultivated for
            - link "dye" [ref=e695] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Dye
            - text: and
            - link "natural gum" [ref=e696] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Natural_gum
            - text: production, respectively.
            - link "Fallow" [ref=e697] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Fallow
            - text: or
            - link "green manure" [ref=e698] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Green_manure
            - text: legume species are cultivated to be tilled back into the soil in order to exploit the high levels of captured atmospheric nitrogen found in the roots of most legumes. Numerous legumes farmed for this purpose include
            - link "Leucaena" [ref=e700] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Leucaena
            - text: ","
            - link "Cyamopsis" [ref=e702] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Cyamopsis
            - text: ", and"
            - link "Sesbania" [ref=e704] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Sesbania
            - text: species. Various legume species are farmed for timber production worldwide, including numerous
            - link "Acacia" [ref=e706] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Acacia
            - text: species and
            - link "Castanospermum australe" [ref=e708] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Castanospermum_australe
            - text: .
            - superscript [ref=e709]:
              - text: "["
              - link "citation needed" [ref=e711] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed
              - text: "]"
          - paragraph [ref=e712]:
            - text: Some legume trees, like the
            - link "honey locust" [ref=e713] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Honey_locust
            - text: (
            - link "Gleditsia" [ref=e715] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Gleditsia
            - text: ) can be used in
            - link "agroforestry" [ref=e716] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Agroforestry
            - text: .
            - superscript [ref=e717]:
              - link "[30]" [ref=e718] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-41"
            - text: Others, including the black locust (
            - link "Robinia pseudoacacia" [ref=e720] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Robinia_pseudoacacia
            - text: ),
            - superscript [ref=e721]:
              - link "[31]" [ref=e722] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-42"
            - text: Kentucky coffeetree (
            - link "Gymnocladus dioicus" [ref=e724] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Kentucky_coffeetree
            - text: ),
            - superscript [ref=e725]:
              - link "[32]" [ref=e726] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-43"
            - generic [ref=e727]:
              - link "Laburnum" [ref=e728] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Laburnum
              - text: ","
            - superscript [ref=e729]:
              - link "[33]" [ref=e730] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-44"
            - text: and the woody climbing vine
            - link "Wisteria" [ref=e732] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Wisteria
            - text: ", have"
            - link "poisonous" [ref=e733] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Poison
            - text: elements.
          - generic [ref=e734]:
            - heading "History" [level=2] [ref=e735]
            - generic [ref=e736]:
              - text: "["
              - link "edit" [ref=e737] [cursor=pointer]:

              - text: "]"
          - paragraph [ref=e738]:
            - link "Neanderthals" [ref=e739] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Neanderthal
            - text: and
            - link "early modern humans" [ref=e740] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Early_modern_humans
            - text: used wild pulses when cooking meals 70,000 to 40,000 years ago.
            - superscript [ref=e741]:
              - link "[34]" [ref=e742] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-45"
            - text: Traces of pulse production have been found around the
            - link "Ravi River" [ref=e743] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Ravi_River
            - text: (
            - link "Punjab" [ref=e744] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Punjab_(region)
            - text: ), the seat of the
            - link "Indus Valley civilisation" [ref=e745] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Indus_Valley_civilisation
            - text: ", from c. 3300 BC. Meanwhile, evidence of lentil cultivation has also been found in Egyptian"
            - link "pyramids" [ref=e746] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Pyramid
            - text: and
            - link "cuneiform" [ref=e747] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Cuneiform
            - link "recipes" [ref=e748] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Recipe
            - text: .
            - superscript [ref=e749]:
              - link "[35]" [ref=e750] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-Albala2007-46"
            - text: Dry pea seeds have been discovered in a Swiss village that are believed to date back to the
            - link "Stone Age" [ref=e751] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Stone_Age
            - text: . Archaeological evidence suggests that these peas must have been grown in the eastern Mediterranean and
            - link "Mesopotamian" [ref=e752] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Mesopotamia
            - text: regions at least 5,000 years ago and in Britain as early as the 11th century.
            - superscript [ref=e753]:
              - link "[36]" [ref=e754] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-b1-47"
            - text: The soybean was domesticated around 5,000 years ago in China from a descendant of the wild vine Glycine soja.
            - superscript [ref=e755]:
              - link "[37]" [ref=e756] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-48"
          - paragraph [ref=e757]:
            - text: The oldest-known domesticated beans in the Americas were found in
            - link "Guitarrero Cave" [ref=e758] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Guitarrero_Cave
            - text: ", an archaeological site in"
            - link "Peru" [ref=e759] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Peru
            - text: ", and dated to around the second millennium BCE."
            - superscript [ref=e760]:
              - link "[38]" [ref=e761] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-Chazan-49"
            - text: Genetic analyses of the common bean Phaseolus show that it originated in
            - link "Mesoamerica" [ref=e762] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Mesoamerica
            - text: ", and subsequently spread southward, along with"
            - link "maize" [ref=e763] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Maize
            - text: and squash, traditional companion crops.
            - superscript [ref=e764]:
              - link "[39]" [ref=e765] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-50"
            - text: In the United States, the domesticated soybean was introduced in 1770 by
            - link "Benjamin Franklin" [ref=e766] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Benjamin_Franklin
            - text: after he sent seeds to Philadelphia from France.
            - superscript [ref=e767]:
              - link "[40]" [ref=e768] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-51"

          - paragraph [ref=e780]:
            - text: The International Year of Pulses 2016 was declared by the
            - link "Sixty-eighth session of the United Nations General Assembly" [ref=e781] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Sixty-eighth_session_of_the_United_Nations_General_Assembly
            - text: .
            - superscript [ref=e782]:
              - link "[41]" [ref=e783] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-iyp-52"
            - text: The
            - link "Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations" [ref=e784] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Food_and_Agriculture_Organization_of_the_United_Nations
            - text: was nominated to facilitate the implementation of the year in collaboration with governments, relevant organizations, non-governmental organizations and other relevant stakeholders. Its aim was to heighten public awareness of the nutritional benefits of pulses as part of
            - link "sustainable food" [ref=e785] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Sustainable_food_systems
            - text: production aimed towards
            - link "food security" [ref=e786] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Food_security
            - text: and
            - link "nutrition" [ref=e787] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Nutrition
            - text: . The year created an opportunity to encourage connections throughout the food chain that would better use pulse-based proteins, further global production of pulses, better use
            - link "crop rotations" [ref=e788] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Crop_rotation
            - text: and address challenges in the global trade of pulses.

function.name: WebSurfer
function.description: A web-focused agent capable of browser-based navigation and a range of online retrieval tasks. Key capabilities include: controlling a browser to visit and extract information from web pages; searching and downloading academic papers from arXiv; looking up content on Wikipedia; downloading YouTube videos (with automatic audio extraction); and general-purpose file downloading from URLs. It can be used to extract textual information from web pages, which can then be passed for further tasks.

function.name: PostgresManager
function.description: A database management agent responsible for inspecting, querying, and analyzing a PostgreSQL database. It can enumerate schemas and database objects, retrieve detailed metadata about tables and other objects, and execute SQL queries (with read-only restrictions when applicable). In addition, it supports query planning and performance analysis, including explaining query execution plans, identifying slow or resource-intensive queries, recommending indexes based on workloads or specific queries, and performing comprehensive database health checks covering caches, indexes, constraints, connections, and maintenance status.

function.name: DocumentAnalyzer
function.description: A comprehensive document-processing agent capable of extracting, analyzing, and structuring content from a wide range of local office files and text formats. Supports CSV/TSV, Word (DOC/DOCX), PowerPoint (PPT/PPTX), Excel (XLS/XLSX), PDF, and diverse text/code files. Provides unified text extraction, table and media extraction, metadata collection, structural analysis, and multi-format output (Markdown/JSON/HTML/Text). Designed to deliver clean, organized results for downstream reasoning and further processing. It can extract embedded media as raw files or generate screenshots for visual spreadsheet elements, which are then passed to specialized agents for further analysis.

function.name: MediaAnalyzer
function.description: A multimedia analysis agent capable of handling local images, audio, and video. It provides OCR extraction, AI-based visual understanding, metadata inspection, audio transcription and trimming, video analysis and summarization, and key-frame extraction. Supports common formats across images (JPG/PNG/GIF/TIFF/WEBP …), audio (MP3/WAV/FLAC/AAC/OGG …), and video (MP4/AVI/MOV/MKV/WEBM …). GIF and video content are processed as multi-frame sequences—similar to video key-frame extraction—while static image formats are analyzed as single frames. Designed to perform assigned multimedia tasks efficiently and return clear, structured results.

function.name: PythonExecutor
function.description: An agent that can execute Python code snippets in an isolated container environment, similar to running cells in a Jupyter Notebook. Its execution is strictly limited to the Python code and data explicitly provided to it. Useful for performing math calculations or demonstrating small code examples.

function.name: Reasoner
function.description: A reasoning specialist agent equipped with a high-capacity reasoning model. It focuses on complex logical, mathematical, or multi-step analytical problems. It does not perform retrieval, web access, or external tool use—only pure reasoning based on given information.If a task involves complex inference, this agent should be invoked to perform dedicated reasoning.Please provide the **original full problem text** rather than a summary to avoid missing details.

function.name: TerminalManager
function.description: An agent that executes shell commands inside an isolated Docker container environment, completely separated from the host system. It performs command-line tasks such as file operations, simple scripting, and other actions suitable for a terminal. It focuses solely on completing the tasks assigned to it through direct command execution.

messages.content:
You are the Caller Agent in a hierarchical multi-agent system.
You do not converse directly with other agents. Instead, you invoke them as tools through function calls.

## ABSOLUTE RULE — read this before anything else
Each agent you invoke is completely isolated. It has NO access to conversation history, NO memory of what previous agents did, and can ONLY see the exact text you write into the tool input field — nothing more.
This means: if a previous agent produced output that the current subtask depends on, you MUST copy that output in full, word for word, into the tool input. There are NO exceptions.
The following are strictly FORBIDDEN in any input:
- "[Full changelog text as above]"
- "[as extracted in step 1]"
- "[see previous output]"
- "[full content as above]"
- Any other placeholder, reference, or shorthand that substitutes for actual content

If you write any such phrase, the receiving agent will see only that phrase — not the actual data — and will produce a completely wrong result. Always paste the real content directly.

## Core workflow
Follow the plan strictly, step by step. For each subtask in the plan, invoke the designated agent (with retries only if needed, see Execution rules), then move to the next subtask. After all subtasks have been processed, immediately produce a detailed summary of the entire execution process and output FINISHED. Do not revisit, re-evaluate, or re-execute any subtask that has already been completed.

## Tool call budget
Your total number of allowed tool calls is strictly limited — only slightly more than the number of subtasks in the plan. This budget is intentionally tight: it is enough to execute every subtask once with occasional retries, but not enough to repeat any subtask repeatedly or restart the entire plan. Excessive retries will consume the budget and prevent later subtasks from being executed at all.

## When invoking a tool, you must provide:
- The subtask content from the plan, passed as faithfully and completely as possible. Do not paraphrase, shorten, or omit details from the original subtask description. You may append clarifications, but never replace or reduce the original subtask content.
- All prior output and user-provided information that this subtask depends on, copied verbatim. No summaries. No references. The full actual text.

Wikipedia's content is governed by **three principal core content policies**:
