messages.content:
You are the WebSurfer agent. You retrieve information from the web by navigating and interacting with pages, exactly as a human would.

## Navigation policy
- Unless the user explicitly provides a URL or names a specific website to visit, always start at google.com. Open Google, type your search query, read the results, and follow links by clicking — do not jump directly to any URL, and do not construct or guess URLs from memory or training data.

## Page size management (critical)
Loading large, unfiltered pages makes it hard to locate relevant information and risks exceeding LLM context length limits. Before loading any page, actively try to reduce its size:
- Use the site's search box with specific keywords rather than browsing index pages.
- Apply any available filters: date range, category, author, language, file type, etc.
- Prefer paginated or scoped views over full listing pages.

## Tool selection
- Prefer specialized tools (ArXiv, Wikipedia, YouTube, direct download, etc.) when they directly match the task. Use browser automation only when no dedicated tool fits.
- Only Google Search is permitted as a search engine.
- For academic paper searches, prefer Google Scholar, arXiv, and DBLP.

## Output
- Produce well-structured, detailed output as required. Extract only what is relevant to the task.
- If you use browser tools to save any content, the browser will store it under the directory: [<PROJECT_ROOT>/tmp/browser_wp]. This is enforced by the browser itself — you only need to report the file path in your output when needed.

Work carefully, efficiently, and stay within your assigned retrieval scope.

          - paragraph [ref=e333]:
            - text: Legumes are widely distributed as the third-largest
            - link "land plant" [ref=e334] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Land_plant
            - text: family in terms of number of species, behind only the
            - link "Orchidaceae" [ref=e335] [cursor=pointer]:

            - text: and
            - link "Asteraceae" [ref=e336] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Asteraceae
            - text: ", with about 751"
            - link "genera" [ref=e337] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Genera
            - text: and some 19,000 known species,
            - superscript [ref=e338]:

            - superscript [ref=e340]:
              - link "[6]" [ref=e341] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-Stevens_2001-17"
            - text: constituting about seven percent of flowering plant species.
            - superscript [ref=e342]:

            - superscript [ref=e344]:

            - link [ref=e357] [cursor=pointer]:

          - paragraph [ref=e363]:
            - text: Many legumes contain
            - link "symbiotic" [ref=e364] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Symbiosis
            - text: bacteria called
            - link "Rhizobia" [ref=e366] [cursor=pointer]:

              - /url: /wiki/Root_nodule
            - text: of their
            - link "root systems" [ref=e368] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Root
            - text: (plants belonging to the genus
            - link "Styphnolobium" [ref=e370] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Styphnolobium
            - text: are one exception to this rule). These bacteria have the special ability of
            - link "fixing nitrogen" [ref=e371] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Nitrogen_fixation
            - text: from atmospheric, molecular nitrogen (N
            - subscript [ref=e372]: "2"
            - text: ) into
            - link "ammonia" [ref=e373] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Ammonia
            - text: (NH
            - subscript [ref=e374]: "3"
            - text: ).
            - superscript [ref=e375]:
              - link "[9]" [ref=e376] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-20"
            - text: "The chemical reaction is:"

              - subscript [ref=e380]: "2"
              - text: + 8 H
              - superscript [ref=e381]: +

              - superscript [ref=e382]: −

              - subscript [ref=e383]: "3"
              - text: + H
              - subscript [ref=e384]: "2"

            - text: Ammonia is converted to another form,
            - link "ammonium" [ref=e386] [cursor=pointer]:

            - text: (
            - generic [ref=e387]:
              - text: NH
              - generic [ref=e388]:
                - generic [ref=e389]: +

            - text: "), usable by (some) plants, by the following reaction:"
          - definition [ref=e392]:
            - generic [ref=e393]:
              - text: NH

              - text: + H
              - superscript [ref=e395]: +
              - text: → NH
              - generic [ref=e396]:
                - generic [ref=e397]: +
                - generic [ref=e398]: "4"
          - paragraph [ref=e399]:
            - text: This arrangement means that the root nodules are sources of nitrogen for legumes, making them relatively rich in nitrogenous
            - link "amino acids" [ref=e400] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Amino_acid
            - text: and
            - link "protein" [ref=e401] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Protein_(nutrient)
            - text: . Nitrogen is therefore a necessary
            - link "ingredient" [ref=e402] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Ingredient
            - text: in the production of proteins.
          - paragraph [ref=e403]:
            - text: When a legume plant dies in the field, for example following the
            - link "harvest" [ref=e404] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Harvest
            - text: ", all of its remaining nitrogen, incorporated into"
            - link "amino acids" [ref=e405] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Amino_acid
            - text: inside the remaining plant parts, is released back into the soil. In the soil, the amino acids are converted to nitrate (
            - generic [ref=e406]:
              - text: "NO"
              - generic [ref=e407]:
                - generic [ref=e408]: −
                - generic [ref=e409]: "3"
            - text: ), making the nitrogen available to other plants, thereby serving as fertilizer for future crops.
            - superscript [ref=e410]:
              - link "[10]" [ref=e411] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-21"
            - superscript [ref=e412]:
              - link "[11]" [ref=e413] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-22"
          - figure "Legumes play a key role in the nitrogen cycle, making nitrates available to other plants in the soil." [ref=e414]:
            - link [ref=e415] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/File:Nitrogen_Cycle.jpg
              - img [ref=e416]
            - generic [ref=e417]:
              - text: Legumes play a key role in the
              - link "nitrogen cycle" [ref=e418] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Nitrogen_cycle
              - text: ", making nitrates available to other plants in the soil."
          - paragraph [ref=e419]:
            - text: In many traditional and
            - link "organic farming" [ref=e420] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Organic_farming
            - text: practices,
            - link "crop rotation" [ref=e421] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Crop_rotation
            - text: or
            - link "polyculture" [ref=e422] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Polyculture
            - text: involving legumes is common. By alternating between legumes and non-legumes, or by growing both together for part of the growing season, the field can receive a sufficient amount of nitrogenous compounds to produce a good result without adding nitrogenous fertilizer. Legumes are often used as
            - link "green manure" [ref=e423] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Green_manure
            - text: .
            - superscript [ref=e424]:
              - text: "["
              - link "citation needed" [ref=e426] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed
              - text: "]"
          - paragraph [ref=e427]:
            - text: Sri Lanka developed the
            - link "polyculture" [ref=e428] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Polyculture
            - text: practice known as coconut-soybean
            - link "intercropping" [ref=e429] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Intercropping
            - text: ". Grain legumes are grown in coconut (Cocos nuficera) groves in two ways: intercropping or as a cash crop. These are grown mainly for their protein, vegetable oil and ability to uphold soil fertility."
            - superscript [ref=e430]:
              - link "[12]" [ref=e431] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-23"
            - text: However, continuous cropping after 3–4 years decrease grain yields significantly.
            - superscript [ref=e432]:
              - link "[13]" [ref=e433] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-24"
          - generic [ref=e434]:
            - heading "Pests and diseases" [level=3] [ref=e435]
            - generic [ref=e436]:
              - text: "["
              - link "edit" [ref=e437] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /w/index.php?title=Legume&action=edit&section=5
              - text: "]"
          - paragraph [ref=e438]:
            - text: A common pest of grain legumes that is noticed in the tropical and subtropical Asia, Africa, Australia and Oceania are minuscule flies that belong to the family
            - link "Agromyzidae" [ref=e440] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Agromyzidae
            - text: ", dubbed \"bean flies\". They are considered to be the most destructive. The host range of these flies is very wide amongst cultivated legumes. Infestation of plants starts from germination through to harvest, and they can destroy an entire crop in early stage."
            - superscript [ref=e441]:
              - link "[14]" [ref=e442] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-25"
            - link "Black bean aphids" [ref=e443] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Black_bean_aphid
            - text: are a serious pest to broad beans and other beans. Common hosts for this pest are fathen, thistle and dock.
            - link "Pea weevil" [ref=e444] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Pea_weevil
            - text: and
            - link "bean weevil" [ref=e445] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Bean_weevil
            - text: damage leaf margins leaving characteristics semi-circular notches.
            - link "Stem nematodes" [ref=e446] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Stem_nematode
            - text: are very widespread but will be found more frequently in areas where host plants are grown.
            - superscript [ref=e447]:
              - link "[15]" [ref=e448] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-26"
          - paragraph [ref=e449]:
            - text: Common legume diseases include

          - paragraph [ref=e479]:
            - text: Abiotic problems include nutrient deficiencies, (nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium, copper, magnesium, manganese, boron, zinc), pollutants (air, water, soil, pesticide injury, fertilizer burn), toxic concentration of minerals, and unfavorable growth conditions.

          - paragraph [ref=e486]:
            - text: Seed viability decreases with longer storage time. Studies of
            - link "vetch" [ref=e487] [cursor=pointer]:

            - text: ","
            - link "broad beans" [ref=e488] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Broad_bean
            - text: ", and peas show that they last about 5 years in storage. Environmental factors that are important in influencing germination are relative humidity and temperature. Two rules apply to moisture content between 5 and 14 percent: the life of the seed will last longer if the storage temperature is reduced by 5 degree Celsius. Secondly, the storage moisture content will decrease if temperature is reduced by 1 degree Celsius."

          - paragraph [ref=e500]:
            - text: Cultivated legumes encompass a diverse range of

            - text: ","
            - link "grain" [ref=e503] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Grain
            - text: ", flowering, pharmaceutical/industrial, fallow/green manure, and timber categories. A notable characteristic of many commercially cultivated legume species is their versatility, often assuming multiple roles concurrently. The extent of these roles is contingent upon the stage of maturity at which they are harvested."

            - link "peanuts" [ref=e524] [cursor=pointer]:

            - superscript [ref=e525]:

                - /url: "#cite_note-31"
          - paragraph [ref=e527]:
            - text: Legumes are a key ingredient in vegan meat and dairy
            - link "substitutes" [ref=e528] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Meat_analogue
            - text: . They are growing in use as a plant-based protein source in the world marketplace.
            - superscript [ref=e529]:

            - superscript [ref=e531]:
              - link "[22]" [ref=e532] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-33"
            - text: Products containing legumes grew by 39% in Europe between 2013 and 2017.
            - superscript [ref=e533]:

                - /url: "#cite_note-eu-growth-34"
          - paragraph [ref=e535]:
            - text: There is a
            - link "common misconception" [ref=e536] [cursor=pointer]:

            - text: that adding salt before cooking prevents them from cooking through. Legumes may not soften because they are old, or because of
            - link "hard water" [ref=e537] [cursor=pointer]:

            - text: or
            - link "acidic" [ref=e538] [cursor=pointer]:

          - paragraph [ref=e548]:
            - text: Legumes are a significant source of
            - link "protein" [ref=e549] [cursor=pointer]:

            - text: ","
            - link "dietary fibre" [ref=e550] [cursor=pointer]:

            - text: ", and"

            - text: ; for example, a 100-gram serving of cooked
            - link "chickpeas" [ref=e553] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Chickpea
            - text: contains 18 percent of the
            - link "Daily Value" [ref=e554] [cursor=pointer]:

            - text: (DV) for protein, 30 percent DV for dietary fiber, 43 percent DV for
            - link "folate" [ref=e555] [cursor=pointer]:

            - text: and 52 percent DV for
            - link "manganese" [ref=e556] [cursor=pointer]:

                - /url: "#cite_note-nd-37"
          - paragraph [ref=e559]:
            - text: Legumes are an excellent source of
            - link "resistant starch" [ref=e560] [cursor=pointer]:

            - text: Forage legumes are of two broad types. Some, like

            - text: ","
            - link "clover" [ref=e579] [cursor=pointer]:

            - link "pasture" [ref=e586] [cursor=pointer]:

            - text: and grazed by livestock. Others, such as
            - link "Leucaena" [ref=e588] [cursor=pointer]:

            - text: or
            - link "Albizia" [ref=e590] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Albizia
            - text: ", are woody shrubs or trees that are either broken down by livestock or regularly cut by humans to provide fodder. Legume-based feeds improve animal performance over a diet of perennial grasses. Factors include larger consumption, faster digestion, and higher"
            - link "feed conversion rate" [ref=e591] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Feed_conversion_rate
            - text: .
            - superscript [ref=e592]:

            - text: can be planted along edges of fields to provide shade for cattle, the leaves and bark are often eaten by cattle. Green manure can be grown between harvesting the main crop and the planting of the next crop.

          - paragraph [ref=e608]:
            - text: Legume species grown for their flowers include
            - link "lupins" [ref=e609] [cursor=pointer]:

            - text: and
            - link "Acacia" [ref=e613] [cursor=pointer]:

            - text: and
            - link "natural gum" [ref=e615] [cursor=pointer]:

            - text: production, respectively.
            - link "Fallow" [ref=e616] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Fallow
            - text: or
            - link "green manure" [ref=e617] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Green_manure
            - text: legume species are cultivated to be tilled back into the soil in order to exploit the high levels of captured atmospheric nitrogen found in the roots of most legumes. Numerous legumes farmed for this purpose include
            - link "Leucaena" [ref=e619] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Leucaena
            - text: ","
            - link "Cyamopsis" [ref=e621] [cursor=pointer]:

            - text: ", and"
            - link "Sesbania" [ref=e623] [cursor=pointer]:

            - link "Acacia" [ref=e625] [cursor=pointer]:

            - text: species and
            - link "Castanospermum australe" [ref=e627] [cursor=pointer]:

            - text: and address challenges in the global trade of pulses.

function.name: mcp_get_article_history
function.description:
Get historical version of a Wikipedia page closest to the specified date.

        This tool provides historical Wikipedia article retrieval with:
        - Date-based version lookup
        - Auto-suggestion support
        - Multi-language support
        - LLM-optimized result formatting
        - Error handling

        If exact date version is not available, returns the closest version before that date.
        Supports auto-suggestion and redirects to handle company name changes or variations.

        Args:
            title: The title of the Wikipedia page
            date: Target date in YYYY/MM/DD format
            language: Language code for Wikipedia
            auto_suggest: Whether to use Wikipedia's auto-suggest and handle redirects
            output_format: Format for the response output

            ActionResponse with historical article content and metadata

messages.content:
You are the WebSurfer agent. You retrieve information from the web by navigating and interacting with pages, exactly as a human would.

## Navigation policy
- Unless the user explicitly provides a URL or names a specific website to visit, always start at google.com. Open Google, type your search query, read the results, and follow links by clicking — do not jump directly to any URL, and do not construct or guess URLs from memory or training data.

## Page size management (critical)
Loading large, unfiltered pages makes it hard to locate relevant information and risks exceeding LLM context length limits. Before loading any page, actively try to reduce its size:
- Use the site's search box with specific keywords rather than browsing index pages.
- Apply any available filters: date range, category, author, language, file type, etc.
- Prefer paginated or scoped views over full listing pages.

## Tool selection
- Prefer specialized tools (ArXiv, Wikipedia, YouTube, direct download, etc.) when they directly match the task. Use browser automation only when no dedicated tool fits.
- Only Google Search is permitted as a search engine.
- For academic paper searches, prefer Google Scholar, arXiv, and DBLP.

## Output
- Produce well-structured, detailed output as required. Extract only what is relevant to the task.
- If you use browser tools to save any content, the browser will store it under the directory: [<PROJECT_ROOT>/tmp/browser_wp]. This is enforced by the browser itself — you only need to report the file path in your output when needed.

Work carefully, efficiently, and stay within your assigned retrieval scope.

          - paragraph [ref=e333]:
            - text: Legumes are widely distributed as the third-largest

            - link "Orchidaceae" [ref=e335] [cursor=pointer]:

            - superscript [ref=e340]:

          - paragraph [ref=e363]:
            - text: Many legumes contain

            - link "root systems" [ref=e368] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Root
            - text: (plants belonging to the genus
            - link "Styphnolobium" [ref=e370] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Styphnolobium
            - text: are one exception to this rule). These bacteria have the special ability of
            - link "fixing nitrogen" [ref=e371] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Nitrogen_fixation
            - text: from atmospheric, molecular nitrogen (N

          - paragraph [ref=e399]:
            - text: This arrangement means that the root nodules are sources of nitrogen for legumes, making them relatively rich in nitrogenous
            - link "amino acids" [ref=e400] [cursor=pointer]:

            - text: and
            - link "protein" [ref=e401] [cursor=pointer]:

            - text: . Nitrogen is therefore a necessary
            - link "ingredient" [ref=e402] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Ingredient
            - text: in the production of proteins.
          - paragraph [ref=e403]:
            - text: When a legume plant dies in the field, for example following the
            - link "harvest" [ref=e404] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Harvest
            - text: ", all of its remaining nitrogen, incorporated into"
            - link "amino acids" [ref=e405] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Amino_acid
            - text: inside the remaining plant parts, is released back into the soil. In the soil, the amino acids are converted to nitrate (
            - generic [ref=e406]:
              - text: "NO"
              - generic [ref=e407]:
                - generic [ref=e408]: −
                - generic [ref=e409]: "3"
            - text: ), making the nitrogen available to other plants, thereby serving as fertilizer for future crops.
            - superscript [ref=e410]:
              - link "[10]" [ref=e411] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-21"
            - superscript [ref=e412]:
              - link "[11]" [ref=e413] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-22"
          - figure "Legumes play a key role in the nitrogen cycle, making nitrates available to other plants in the soil." [ref=e414]:

            - generic [ref=e417]:
              - text: Legumes play a key role in the
              - link "nitrogen cycle" [ref=e418] [cursor=pointer]:

              - text: ", making nitrates available to other plants in the soil."
          - paragraph [ref=e419]:
            - text: In many traditional and
            - link "organic farming" [ref=e420] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Organic_farming
            - text: practices,
            - link "crop rotation" [ref=e421] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Crop_rotation
            - text: or
            - link "polyculture" [ref=e422] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Polyculture
            - text: involving legumes is common. By alternating between legumes and non-legumes, or by growing both together for part of the growing season, the field can receive a sufficient amount of nitrogenous compounds to produce a good result without adding nitrogenous fertilizer. Legumes are often used as
            - link "green manure" [ref=e423] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Green_manure
            - text: .
            - superscript [ref=e424]:
              - text: "["
              - link "citation needed" [ref=e426] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed
              - text: "]"
          - paragraph [ref=e427]:
            - text: Sri Lanka developed the
            - link "polyculture" [ref=e428] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Polyculture
            - text: practice known as coconut-soybean
            - link "intercropping" [ref=e429] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Intercropping
            - text: ". Grain legumes are grown in coconut (Cocos nuficera) groves in two ways: intercropping or as a cash crop. These are grown mainly for their protein, vegetable oil and ability to uphold soil fertility."
            - superscript [ref=e430]:
              - link "[12]" [ref=e431] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-23"
            - text: However, continuous cropping after 3–4 years decrease grain yields significantly.
            - superscript [ref=e432]:
              - link "[13]" [ref=e433] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-24"

              - text: "]"
          - paragraph [ref=e438]:
            - text: A common pest of grain legumes that is noticed in the tropical and subtropical Asia, Africa, Australia and Oceania are minuscule flies that belong to the family
            - link "Agromyzidae" [ref=e440] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Agromyzidae
            - text: ", dubbed \"bean flies\". They are considered to be the most destructive. The host range of these flies is very wide amongst cultivated legumes. Infestation of plants starts from germination through to harvest, and they can destroy an entire crop in early stage."
            - superscript [ref=e441]:
              - link "[14]" [ref=e442] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-25"
            - link "Black bean aphids" [ref=e443] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Black_bean_aphid
            - text: are a serious pest to broad beans and other beans. Common hosts for this pest are fathen, thistle and dock.
            - link "Pea weevil" [ref=e444] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Pea_weevil
            - text: and
            - link "bean weevil" [ref=e445] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Bean_weevil
            - text: damage leaf margins leaving characteristics semi-circular notches.
            - link "Stem nematodes" [ref=e446] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Stem_nematode
            - text: are very widespread but will be found more frequently in areas where host plants are grown.
            - superscript [ref=e447]:
              - link "[15]" [ref=e448] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-26"

          - paragraph [ref=e486]:
            - text: Seed viability decreases with longer storage time. Studies of
            - link "vetch" [ref=e487] [cursor=pointer]:

            - text: ","
            - link "broad beans" [ref=e488] [cursor=pointer]:

            - text: ", and peas show that they last about 5 years in storage. Environmental factors that are important in influencing germination are relative humidity and temperature. Two rules apply to moisture content between 5 and 14 percent: the life of the seed will last longer if the storage temperature is reduced by 5 degree Celsius. Secondly, the storage moisture content will decrease if temperature is reduced by 1 degree Celsius."

            - text: Grain legumes are cultivated for their seeds,
            - superscript [ref=e518]:
              - link "[19]" [ref=e519] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-crops-30"
            - text: for humans and animals to eat, or for oils for industrial uses. Grain legumes include
            - link "beans" [ref=e520] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Bean
            - text: ","
            - link "lentils" [ref=e521] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Lentil
            - text: ","
            - link "lupins" [ref=e522] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Lupin
            - text: ","
            - link "peas" [ref=e523] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Pea
            - text: ", and"
            - link "peanuts" [ref=e524] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Peanut
            - text: .
            - superscript [ref=e525]:
              - link "[20]" [ref=e526] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-31"
          - paragraph [ref=e527]:
            - text: Legumes are a key ingredient in vegan meat and dairy
            - link "substitutes" [ref=e528] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Meat_analogue
            - text: . They are growing in use as a plant-based protein source in the world marketplace.
            - superscript [ref=e529]:
              - link "[21]" [ref=e530] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-sc-australian-32"
            - superscript [ref=e531]:
              - link "[22]" [ref=e532] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-33"
            - text: Products containing legumes grew by 39% in Europe between 2013 and 2017.
            - superscript [ref=e533]:
              - link "[23]" [ref=e534] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-eu-growth-34"
          - paragraph [ref=e535]:
            - text: There is a
            - link "common misconception" [ref=e536] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/List_of_common_misconceptions
            - text: that adding salt before cooking prevents them from cooking through. Legumes may not soften because they are old, or because of
            - link "hard water" [ref=e537] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Hard_water
            - text: or
            - link "acidic" [ref=e538] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Acid
            - text: ingredients in the pot; salting before cooking results in better
            - link "seasoning" [ref=e539] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Seasoning
            - text: .
            - superscript [ref=e540]:
              - link "[24]" [ref=e541] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-35"
            - superscript [ref=e542]:
              - link "[25]" [ref=e543] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-36"
          - generic [ref=e544]:
            - heading "Nutritional value" [level=4] [ref=e545]
            - generic [ref=e546]:
              - text: "["
              - link "edit" [ref=e547] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /w/index.php?title=Legume&action=edit&section=9
              - text: "]"
          - paragraph [ref=e548]:
            - text: Legumes are a significant source of
            - link "protein" [ref=e549] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Protein_(nutrient)
            - text: ","
            - link "dietary fibre" [ref=e550] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Dietary_fiber
            - text: ","
            - link "carbohydrates" [ref=e551] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Carbohydrate
            - text: ", and"
            - link "dietary minerals" [ref=e552] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Dietary_minerals
            - text: ; for example, a 100-gram serving of cooked
            - link "chickpeas" [ref=e553] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Chickpea
            - text: contains 18 percent of the
            - link "Daily Value" [ref=e554] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Daily_Value
            - text: (DV) for protein, 30 percent DV for dietary fiber, 43 percent DV for
            - link "folate" [ref=e555] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Folate
            - text: and 52 percent DV for
            - link "manganese" [ref=e556] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Manganese
            - text: .
            - superscript [ref=e557]:
              - link "[26]" [ref=e558] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-nd-37"
          - paragraph [ref=e559]:
            - text: Legumes are an excellent source of
            - link "resistant starch" [ref=e560] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Resistant_starch
            - text: ; this is broken down by
            - link "bacteria" [ref=e561] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Gut_flora
            - text: in the
            - link "large intestine" [ref=e562] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Large_intestine
            - text: to produce
            - link "short-chain fatty acids" [ref=e563] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Short-chain_fatty_acid
            - text: (such as
            - link "butyrate" [ref=e564] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Butyrate
            - text: ) used by intestinal cells for
            - link "food energy" [ref=e565] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Food_energy
            - text: .
            - superscript [ref=e566]:
              - link "[27]" [ref=e567] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-38"
          - generic [ref=e568]:

              - link "clover" [ref=e576] [cursor=pointer]:

              - text: ", a forage crop"
          - paragraph [ref=e577]:
            - text: Forage legumes are of two broad types. Some, like
            - link "alfalfa" [ref=e578] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Alfalfa
            - text: ","
            - link "clover" [ref=e579] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Clover
            - text: ", vetch ("
            - link "Vicia" [ref=e581] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Vicia
            - text: ), stylo (
            - link "Stylosanthes" [ref=e583] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Stylosanthes
            - text: ), or
            - link "Arachis" [ref=e585] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Arachis
            - text: ", are sown in"
            - link "pasture" [ref=e586] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Pasture
            - text: and grazed by livestock. Others, such as
            - link "Leucaena" [ref=e588] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Leucaena
            - text: or
            - link "Albizia" [ref=e590] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Albizia
            - text: ", are woody shrubs or trees that are either broken down by livestock or regularly cut by humans to provide fodder. Legume-based feeds improve animal performance over a diet of perennial grasses. Factors include larger consumption, faster digestion, and higher"
            - link "feed conversion rate" [ref=e591] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Feed_conversion_rate
            - text: .
            - superscript [ref=e592]:
              - link "[28]" [ref=e593] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-39"
          - paragraph [ref=e594]:
            - text: The type of crop grown for animal rearing depends on the farming system. In cattle rearing, legume trees such as
            - link "Gliricidia sepium" [ref=e596] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Gliricidia_sepium
            - text: can be planted along edges of fields to provide shade for cattle, the leaves and bark are often eaten by cattle. Green manure can be grown between harvesting the main crop and the planting of the next crop.
            - superscript [ref=e597]:
              - link "[29]" [ref=e598] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-40"
          - generic [ref=e599]:
            - heading "Other uses" [level=3] [ref=e600]
            - generic [ref=e601]:
              - text: "["
              - link "edit" [ref=e602] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /w/index.php?title=Legume&action=edit&section=11
              - text: "]"
          - figure "Lupin flower garden" [ref=e603]:
            - link [ref=e604] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/File:Flower_garden_in_Ushuaia_(5542996965).jpg
              - img [ref=e605]
            - generic [ref=e606]:
              - link "Lupin" [ref=e607] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Lupin
              - text: flower garden
          - paragraph [ref=e608]:
            - text: Legume species grown for their flowers include
            - link "lupins" [ref=e609] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Lupin
            - text: ", which are farmed commercially for their blooms as well as being popular in gardens worldwide. Industrially farmed legumes include"
            - link "Indigofera" [ref=e611] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Indigofera
            - text: and
            - link "Acacia" [ref=e613] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Acacia
            - text: species, which are cultivated for
            - link "dye" [ref=e614] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Dye
            - text: and
            - link "natural gum" [ref=e615] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Natural_gum
            - text: production, respectively.
            - link "Fallow" [ref=e616] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Fallow
            - text: or
            - link "green manure" [ref=e617] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Green_manure
            - text: legume species are cultivated to be tilled back into the soil in order to exploit the high levels of captured atmospheric nitrogen found in the roots of most legumes. Numerous legumes farmed for this purpose include
            - link "Leucaena" [ref=e619] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Leucaena
            - text: ","
            - link "Cyamopsis" [ref=e621] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Cyamopsis
            - text: ", and"
            - link "Sesbania" [ref=e623] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Sesbania
            - text: species. Various legume species are farmed for timber production worldwide, including numerous
            - link "Acacia" [ref=e625] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Acacia
            - text: species and
            - link "Castanospermum australe" [ref=e627] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Castanospermum_australe
            - text: .
            - superscript [ref=e628]:
              - text: "["
              - link "citation needed" [ref=e630] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed
              - text: "]"
          - paragraph [ref=e631]:
            - text: Some legume trees, like the
            - link "honey locust" [ref=e632] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Honey_locust
            - text: (
            - link "Gleditsia" [ref=e634] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Gleditsia
            - text: ) can be used in
            - link "agroforestry" [ref=e635] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Agroforestry
            - text: .
            - superscript [ref=e636]:
              - link "[30]" [ref=e637] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-41"
            - text: Others, including the black locust (
            - link "Robinia pseudoacacia" [ref=e639] [cursor=pointer]:

            - link "Gymnocladus dioicus" [ref=e643] [cursor=pointer]:

            - text: ),
            - superscript [ref=e644]:

            - text: and
            - link "early modern humans" [ref=e659] [cursor=pointer]:

            - text: used wild pulses when cooking meals 70,000 to 40,000 years ago.
            - superscript [ref=e660]:
              - link "[34]" [ref=e661] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-45"
            - text: Traces of pulse production have been found around the
            - link "Ravi River" [ref=e662] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Ravi_River
            - text: (
            - link "Punjab" [ref=e663] [cursor=pointer]:

            - text: ), the seat of the
            - link "Indus Valley civilisation" [ref=e664] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Indus_Valley_civilisation
            - text: ", from c. 3300 BC. Meanwhile, evidence of lentil cultivation has also been found in Egyptian"
            - link "pyramids" [ref=e665] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Pyramid
            - text: and
            - link "cuneiform" [ref=e666] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Cuneiform
            - link "recipes" [ref=e667] [cursor=pointer]:

            - text: .
            - superscript [ref=e668]:
              - link "[35]" [ref=e669] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-Albala2007-46"
            - text: Dry pea seeds have been discovered in a Swiss village that are believed to date back to the
            - link "Stone Age" [ref=e670] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Stone_Age
            - text: . Archaeological evidence suggests that these peas must have been grown in the eastern Mediterranean and
            - link "Mesopotamian" [ref=e671] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Mesopotamia
            - text: regions at least 5,000 years ago and in Britain as early as the 11th century.
            - superscript [ref=e672]:
              - link "[36]" [ref=e673] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-b1-47"
            - text: The soybean was domesticated around 5,000 years ago in China from a descendant of the wild vine Glycine soja.
            - superscript [ref=e674]:
              - link "[37]" [ref=e675] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-48"
          - paragraph [ref=e676]:
            - text: The oldest-known domesticated beans in the Americas were found in
            - link "Guitarrero Cave" [ref=e677] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Guitarrero_Cave
            - text: ", an archaeological site in"
            - link "Peru" [ref=e678] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Peru
            - text: ", and dated to around the second millennium BCE."
            - superscript [ref=e679]:
              - link "[38]" [ref=e680] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-Chazan-49"
            - text: Genetic analyses of the common bean Phaseolus show that it originated in
            - link "Mesoamerica" [ref=e681] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Mesoamerica
            - text: ", and subsequently spread southward, along with"
            - link "maize" [ref=e682] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Maize
            - text: and squash, traditional companion crops.
            - superscript [ref=e683]:
              - link "[39]" [ref=e684] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-50"
            - text: In the United States, the domesticated soybean was introduced in 1770 by
            - link "Benjamin Franklin" [ref=e685] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Benjamin_Franklin
            - text: after he sent seeds to Philadelphia from France.

            - text: The International Year of Pulses 2016 was declared by the

              - link "[41]" [ref=e702] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-iyp-52"
            - text: The
            - link "Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations" [ref=e703] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Food_and_Agriculture_Organization_of_the_United_Nations
            - text: was nominated to facilitate the implementation of the year in collaboration with governments, relevant organizations, non-governmental organizations and other relevant stakeholders. Its aim was to heighten public awareness of the nutritional benefits of pulses as part of
            - link "sustainable food" [ref=e704] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Sustainable_food_systems
            - text: production aimed towards
            - link "food security" [ref=e705] [cursor=pointer]:

            - text: and
            - link "nutrition" [ref=e706] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Nutrition

            - link "crop rotations" [ref=e707] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Crop_rotation
            - text: and address challenges in the global trade of pulses.

## Page size management (critical)
Loading large, unfiltered pages makes it hard to locate relevant information and risks exceeding LLM context length limits. Before loading any page, actively try to reduce its size:
- Use the site's search box with specific keywords rather than browsing index pages.
- Apply any available filters: date range, category, author, language, file type, etc.
- Prefer paginated or scoped views over full listing pages.

- Only Google Search is permitted as a search engine.
- For academic paper searches, prefer Google Scholar, arXiv, and DBLP.

Work carefully, efficiently, and stay within your assigned retrieval scope.

            - text: are one exception to this rule). These bacteria have the special ability of
            - link "fixing nitrogen" [ref=e371] [cursor=pointer]:

          - paragraph [ref=e399]:
            - text: This arrangement means that the root nodules are sources of nitrogen for legumes, making them relatively rich in nitrogenous
            - link "amino acids" [ref=e400] [cursor=pointer]:

            - text: and
            - link "protein" [ref=e401] [cursor=pointer]:

            - link "ingredient" [ref=e402] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Ingredient
            - text: in the production of proteins.
          - paragraph [ref=e403]:
            - text: When a legume plant dies in the field, for example following the
            - link "harvest" [ref=e404] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Harvest
            - text: ", all of its remaining nitrogen, incorporated into"
            - link "amino acids" [ref=e405] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Amino_acid
            - text: inside the remaining plant parts, is released back into the soil. In the soil, the amino acids are converted to nitrate (
            - generic [ref=e406]:
              - text: "NO"
              - generic [ref=e407]:
                - generic [ref=e408]: −
                - generic [ref=e409]: "3"
            - text: ), making the nitrogen available to other plants, thereby serving as fertilizer for future crops.
            - superscript [ref=e410]:

                - /url: "#cite_note-21"
            - superscript [ref=e412]:

          - paragraph [ref=e419]:
            - text: In many traditional and
            - link "organic farming" [ref=e420] [cursor=pointer]:

            - text: practices,

By alternating between legumes and non-legumes, or by growing both together for part of the growing season, the field can receive a sufficient amount of nitrogenous compounds to produce a good result without adding nitrogenous fertilizer. Legumes are often used as
            - link "green manure" [ref=e423] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Green_manure
            - text: .

              - text: "]"
          - paragraph [ref=e427]:
            - text: Sri Lanka developed the
            - link "polyculture" [ref=e428] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Polyculture
            - text: practice known as coconut-soybean
            - link "intercropping" [ref=e429] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Intercropping
            - text: ". Grain legumes are grown in coconut (Cocos nuficera) groves in two ways: intercropping or as a cash crop. These are grown mainly for their protein, vegetable oil and ability to uphold soil fertility."
            - superscript [ref=e430]:
              - link "[12]" [ref=e431] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-23"
            - text: However, continuous cropping after 3–4 years decrease grain yields significantly.

          - paragraph [ref=e438]:
            - text: A common pest of grain legumes that is noticed in the tropical and subtropical Asia, Africa, Australia and Oceania are minuscule flies that belong to the family
            - link "Agromyzidae" [ref=e440] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Agromyzidae
            - text: ", dubbed \"bean flies\". They are considered to be the most destructive. The host range of these flies is very wide amongst cultivated legumes. Infestation of plants starts from germination through to harvest, and they can destroy an entire crop in early stage."
            - superscript [ref=e441]:
              - link "[14]" [ref=e442] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-25"
            - link "Black bean aphids" [ref=e443] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Black_bean_aphid
            - text: are a serious pest to broad beans and other beans. Common hosts for this pest are fathen, thistle and dock.
            - link "Pea weevil" [ref=e444] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Pea_weevil
            - text: and
            - link "bean weevil" [ref=e445] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Bean_weevil
            - text: damage leaf margins leaving characteristics semi-circular notches.
            - link "Stem nematodes" [ref=e446] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Stem_nematode
            - text: are very widespread but will be found more frequently in areas where host plants are grown.

          - paragraph [ref=e486]:
            - text: Seed viability decreases with longer storage time. Studies of
            - link "vetch" [ref=e487] [cursor=pointer]:

            - text: ","
            - link "broad beans" [ref=e488] [cursor=pointer]:

            - text: ", and peas show that they last about 5 years in storage. Environmental factors that are important in influencing germination are relative humidity and temperature. Two rules apply to moisture content between 5 and 14 percent: the life of the seed will last longer if the storage temperature is reduced by 5 degree Celsius. Secondly, the storage moisture content will decrease if temperature is reduced by 1 degree Celsius."

            - text: ","

            - text: ", and"

            - text: ; for example, a 100-gram serving of cooked
            - link "chickpeas" [ref=e553] [cursor=pointer]:

            - text: contains 18 percent of the
            - link "Daily Value" [ref=e554] [cursor=pointer]:

                - /url: "#cite_note-nd-37"
          - paragraph [ref=e559]:
            - text: Legumes are an excellent source of
            - link "resistant starch" [ref=e560] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Resistant_starch
            - text: ; this is broken down by
            - link "bacteria" [ref=e561] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Gut_flora
            - text: in the
            - link "large intestine" [ref=e562] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Large_intestine
            - text: to produce
            - link "short-chain fatty acids" [ref=e563] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Short-chain_fatty_acid
            - text: (such as
            - link "butyrate" [ref=e564] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Butyrate
            - text: ) used by intestinal cells for
            - link "food energy" [ref=e565] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Food_energy
            - text: .
            - superscript [ref=e566]:
              - link "[27]" [ref=e567] [cursor=pointer]:

          - generic [ref=e568]:
            - heading "Forage" [level=3] [ref=e569]
            - generic [ref=e570]:
              - text: "["
              - link "edit" [ref=e571] [cursor=pointer]:

              - text: "]"
          - figure "White clover, a forage crop" [ref=e572]:
            - link [ref=e573] [cursor=pointer]:

            - generic [ref=e575]:

              - link "clover" [ref=e576] [cursor=pointer]:

              - text: ", a forage crop"
          - paragraph [ref=e577]:
            - text: Forage legumes are of two broad types. Some, like
            - link "alfalfa" [ref=e578] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Alfalfa
            - text: ","
            - link "clover" [ref=e579] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Clover
            - text: ", vetch ("
            - link "Vicia" [ref=e581] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Vicia
            - text: ), stylo (
            - link "Stylosanthes" [ref=e583] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Stylosanthes
            - text: ), or
            - link "Arachis" [ref=e585] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Arachis
            - text: ", are sown in"
            - link "pasture" [ref=e586] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Pasture
            - text: and grazed by livestock. Others, such as
            - link "Leucaena" [ref=e588] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Leucaena
            - text: or
            - link "Albizia" [ref=e590] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Albizia
            - text: ", are woody shrubs or trees that are either broken down by livestock or regularly cut by humans to provide fodder. Legume-based feeds improve animal performance over a diet of perennial grasses. Factors include larger consumption, faster digestion, and higher"
            - link "feed conversion rate" [ref=e591] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Feed_conversion_rate
            - text: .
            - superscript [ref=e592]:
              - link "[28]" [ref=e593] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-39"
          - paragraph [ref=e594]:
            - text: The type of crop grown for animal rearing depends on the farming system. In cattle rearing, legume trees such as
            - link "Gliricidia sepium" [ref=e596] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Gliricidia_sepium
            - text: can be planted along edges of fields to provide shade for cattle, the leaves and bark are often eaten by cattle. Green manure can be grown between harvesting the main crop and the planting of the next crop.
            - superscript [ref=e597]:
              - link "[29]" [ref=e598] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-40"
          - generic [ref=e599]:
            - heading "Other uses" [level=3] [ref=e600]
            - generic [ref=e601]:
              - text: "["
              - link "edit" [ref=e602] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /w/index.php?title=Legume&action=edit&section=11
              - text: "]"
          - figure "Lupin flower garden" [ref=e603]:
            - link [ref=e604] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/File:Flower_garden_in_Ushuaia_(5542996965).jpg
              - img [ref=e605]
            - generic [ref=e606]:
              - link "Lupin" [ref=e607] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Lupin
              - text: flower garden
          - paragraph [ref=e608]:
            - text: Legume species grown for their flowers include
            - link "lupins" [ref=e609] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Lupin
            - text: ", which are farmed commercially for their blooms as well as being popular in gardens worldwide. Industrially farmed legumes include"
            - link "Indigofera" [ref=e611] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Indigofera
            - text: and
            - link "Acacia" [ref=e613] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Acacia
            - text: species, which are cultivated for
            - link "dye" [ref=e614] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Dye
            - text: and
            - link "natural gum" [ref=e615] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Natural_gum
            - text: production, respectively.
            - link "Fallow" [ref=e616] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Fallow
            - text: or
            - link "green manure" [ref=e617] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Green_manure
            - text: legume species are cultivated to be tilled back into the soil in order to exploit the high levels of captured atmospheric nitrogen found in the roots of most legumes. Numerous legumes farmed for this purpose include
            - link "Leucaena" [ref=e619] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Leucaena
            - text: ","
            - link "Cyamopsis" [ref=e621] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Cyamopsis
            - text: ", and"
            - link "Sesbania" [ref=e623] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Sesbania
            - text: species. Various legume species are farmed for timber production worldwide, including numerous
            - link "Acacia" [ref=e625] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Acacia
            - text: species and
            - link "Castanospermum australe" [ref=e627] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Castanospermum_australe
            - text: .
            - superscript [ref=e628]:
              - text: "["
              - link "citation needed" [ref=e630] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed
              - text: "]"
          - paragraph [ref=e631]:
            - text: Some legume trees, like the
            - link "honey locust" [ref=e632] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Honey_locust
            - text: (
            - link "Gleditsia" [ref=e634] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Gleditsia
            - text: ) can be used in
            - link "agroforestry" [ref=e635] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Agroforestry
            - text: .
            - superscript [ref=e636]:
              - link "[30]" [ref=e637] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-41"
            - text: Others, including the black locust (
            - link "Robinia pseudoacacia" [ref=e639] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Robinia_pseudoacacia
            - text: ),
            - superscript [ref=e640]:
              - link "[31]" [ref=e641] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-42"
            - text: Kentucky coffeetree (
            - link "Gymnocladus dioicus" [ref=e643] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Kentucky_coffeetree
            - text: ),
            - superscript [ref=e644]:
              - link "[32]" [ref=e645] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-43"
            - generic [ref=e646]:
              - link "Laburnum" [ref=e647] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Laburnum
              - text: ","
            - superscript [ref=e648]:
              - link "[33]" [ref=e649] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-44"
            - text: and the woody climbing vine
            - link "Wisteria" [ref=e651] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Wisteria
            - text: ", have"
            - link "poisonous" [ref=e652] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Poison
            - text: elements.
          - generic [ref=e653]:
            - heading "History" [level=2] [ref=e654]

              - text: "["

          - paragraph [ref=e657]:
            - link "Neanderthals" [ref=e658] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Neanderthal
            - text: and
            - link "early modern humans" [ref=e659] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Early_modern_humans
            - text: used wild pulses when cooking meals 70,000 to 40,000 years ago.
            - superscript [ref=e660]:
              - link "[34]" [ref=e661] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-45"
            - text: Traces of pulse production have been found around the
            - link "Ravi River" [ref=e662] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Ravi_River
            - text: (
            - link "Punjab" [ref=e663] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Punjab_(region)
            - text: ), the seat of the
            - link "Indus Valley civilisation" [ref=e664] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Indus_Valley_civilisation
            - text: ", from c. 3300 BC. Meanwhile, evidence of lentil cultivation has also been found in Egyptian"
            - link "pyramids" [ref=e665] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Pyramid
            - text: and
            - link "cuneiform" [ref=e666] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Cuneiform
            - link "recipes" [ref=e667] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Recipe
            - text: .
            - superscript [ref=e668]:
              - link "[35]" [ref=e669] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-Albala2007-46"
            - text: Dry pea seeds have been discovered in a Swiss village that are believed to date back to the
            - link "Stone Age" [ref=e670] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Stone_Age
            - text: . Archaeological evidence suggests that these peas must have been grown in the eastern Mediterranean and
            - link "Mesopotamian" [ref=e671] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Mesopotamia
            - text: regions at least 5,000 years ago and in Britain as early as the 11th century.
            - superscript [ref=e672]:
              - link "[36]" [ref=e673] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-b1-47"
            - text: The soybean was domesticated around 5,000 years ago in China from a descendant of the wild vine Glycine soja.
            - superscript [ref=e674]:
              - link "[37]" [ref=e675] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-48"
          - paragraph [ref=e676]:
            - text: The oldest-known domesticated beans in the Americas were found in
            - link "Guitarrero Cave" [ref=e677] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Guitarrero_Cave
            - text: ", an archaeological site in"
            - link "Peru" [ref=e678] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Peru
            - text: ", and dated to around the second millennium BCE."
            - superscript [ref=e679]:
              - link "[38]" [ref=e680] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-Chazan-49"
            - text: Genetic analyses of the common bean Phaseolus show that it originated in
            - link "Mesoamerica" [ref=e681] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Mesoamerica
            - text: ", and subsequently spread southward, along with"
            - link "maize" [ref=e682] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Maize
            - text: and squash, traditional companion crops.
            - superscript [ref=e683]:
              - link "[39]" [ref=e684] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-50"
            - text: In the United States, the domesticated soybean was introduced in 1770 by
            - link "Benjamin Franklin" [ref=e685] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Benjamin_Franklin
            - text: after he sent seeds to Philadelphia from France.
            - superscript [ref=e686]:
              - link "[40]" [ref=e687] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-51"

          - paragraph [ref=e699]:
            - text: The International Year of Pulses 2016 was declared by the
            - link "Sixty-eighth session of the United Nations General Assembly" [ref=e700] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Sixty-eighth_session_of_the_United_Nations_General_Assembly
            - text: .
            - superscript [ref=e701]:
              - link "[41]" [ref=e702] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-iyp-52"
            - text: The
            - link "Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations" [ref=e703] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Food_and_Agriculture_Organization_of_the_United_Nations
            - text: was nominated to facilitate the implementation of the year in collaboration with governments, relevant organizations, non-governmental organizations and other relevant stakeholders. Its aim was to heighten public awareness of the nutritional benefits of pulses as part of
            - link "sustainable food" [ref=e704] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Sustainable_food_systems
            - text: production aimed towards
            - link "food security" [ref=e705] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Food_security
            - text: and
            - link "nutrition" [ref=e706] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Nutrition
            - text: . The year created an opportunity to encourage connections throughout the food chain that would better use pulse-based proteins, further global production of pulses, better use
            - link "crop rotations" [ref=e707] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Crop_rotation
            - text: and address challenges in the global trade of pulses.

          - paragraph [ref=e399]:
            - text: This arrangement means that the root nodules are sources of nitrogen for legumes, making them relatively rich in nitrogenous

          - paragraph [ref=e403]:
            - text: When a legume plant dies in the field, for example following the
            - link "harvest" [ref=e404] [cursor=pointer]:

            - text: ", all of its remaining nitrogen, incorporated into"
            - link "amino acids" [ref=e405] [cursor=pointer]:

            - text: inside the remaining plant parts, is released back into the soil. In the soil, the amino acids are converted to nitrate (
            - generic [ref=e406]:
              - text: "NO"
              - generic [ref=e407]:

            - text: ), making the nitrogen available to other plants, thereby serving as fertilizer for future crops.
            - superscript [ref=e410]:

            - superscript [ref=e412]:

            - text: In many traditional and

By alternating between legumes and non-legumes, or by growing both together for part of the growing season, the field can receive a sufficient amount of nitrogenous compounds to produce a good result without adding nitrogenous fertilizer. Legumes are often used as
            - link "green manure" [ref=e423] [cursor=pointer]:

              - text: "]"
          - paragraph [ref=e427]:
            - text: Sri Lanka developed the
            - link "polyculture" [ref=e428] [cursor=pointer]:

            - text: practice known as coconut-soybean
            - link "intercropping" [ref=e429] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Intercropping
            - text: ". Grain legumes are grown in coconut (Cocos nuficera) groves in two ways: intercropping or as a cash crop. These are grown mainly for their protein, vegetable oil and ability to uphold soil fertility."
            - superscript [ref=e430]:
              - link "[12]" [ref=e431] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-23"
            - text: However, continuous cropping after 3–4 years decrease grain yields significantly.

          - paragraph [ref=e438]:

            - link "Agromyzidae" [ref=e440] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Agromyzidae
            - text: ", dubbed \"bean flies\". They are considered to be the most destructive. The host range of these flies is very wide amongst cultivated legumes. Infestation of plants starts from germination through to harvest, and they can destroy an entire crop in early stage."
            - superscript [ref=e441]:
              - link "[14]" [ref=e442] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-25"
            - link "Black bean aphids" [ref=e443] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Black_bean_aphid
            - text: are a serious pest to broad beans and other beans. Common hosts for this pest are fathen, thistle and dock.

            - text: and
            - link "bean weevil" [ref=e445] [cursor=pointer]:

            - text: damage leaf margins leaving characteristics semi-circular notches.

            - text: are very widespread but will be found more frequently in areas where host plants are grown.

          - paragraph [ref=e486]:

            - link "Arachis" [ref=e585] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Arachis
            - text: ", are sown in"
            - link "pasture" [ref=e586] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Pasture
            - text: and grazed by livestock. Others, such as
            - link "Leucaena" [ref=e588] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Leucaena
            - text: or
            - link "Albizia" [ref=e590] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Albizia
            - text: ", are woody shrubs or trees that are either broken down by livestock or regularly cut by humans to provide fodder. Legume-based feeds improve animal performance over a diet of perennial grasses. Factors include larger consumption, faster digestion, and higher"
            - link "feed conversion rate" [ref=e591] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Feed_conversion_rate
            - text: .
            - superscript [ref=e592]:
              - link "[28]" [ref=e593] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-39"
          - paragraph [ref=e594]:
            - text: The type of crop grown for animal rearing depends on the farming system. In cattle rearing, legume trees such as
            - link "Gliricidia sepium" [ref=e596] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Gliricidia_sepium
            - text: can be planted along edges of fields to provide shade for cattle, the leaves and bark are often eaten by cattle. Green manure can be grown between harvesting the main crop and the planting of the next crop.
            - superscript [ref=e597]:
              - link "[29]" [ref=e598] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-40"
          - generic [ref=e599]:
            - heading "Other uses" [level=3] [ref=e600]
            - generic [ref=e601]:
              - text: "["
              - link "edit" [ref=e602] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /w/index.php?title=Legume&action=edit&section=11
              - text: "]"
          - figure "Lupin flower garden" [ref=e603]:
            - link [ref=e604] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/File:Flower_garden_in_Ushuaia_(5542996965).jpg
              - img [ref=e605]
            - generic [ref=e606]:
              - link "Lupin" [ref=e607] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Lupin
              - text: flower garden
          - paragraph [ref=e608]:
            - text: Legume species grown for their flowers include
            - link "lupins" [ref=e609] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Lupin
            - text: ", which are farmed commercially for their blooms as well as being popular in gardens worldwide. Industrially farmed legumes include"
            - link "Indigofera" [ref=e611] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Indigofera
            - text: and
            - link "Acacia" [ref=e613] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Acacia
            - text: species, which are cultivated for
            - link "dye" [ref=e614] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Dye
            - text: and
            - link "natural gum" [ref=e615] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Natural_gum
            - text: production, respectively.
            - link "Fallow" [ref=e616] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Fallow
            - text: or
            - link "green manure" [ref=e617] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Green_manure
            - text: legume species are cultivated to be tilled back into the soil in order to exploit the high levels of captured atmospheric nitrogen found in the roots of most legumes. Numerous legumes farmed for this purpose include
            - link "Leucaena" [ref=e619] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Leucaena
            - text: ","
            - link "Cyamopsis" [ref=e621] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Cyamopsis
            - text: ", and"
            - link "Sesbania" [ref=e623] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Sesbania
            - text: species. Various legume species are farmed for timber production worldwide, including numerous
            - link "Acacia" [ref=e625] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Acacia
            - text: species and
            - link "Castanospermum australe" [ref=e627] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Castanospermum_australe
            - text: .
            - superscript [ref=e628]:
              - text: "["
              - link "citation needed" [ref=e630] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed
              - text: "]"
          - paragraph [ref=e631]:
            - text: Some legume trees, like the
            - link "honey locust" [ref=e632] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Honey_locust
            - text: (
            - link "Gleditsia" [ref=e634] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Gleditsia
            - text: ) can be used in
            - link "agroforestry" [ref=e635] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Agroforestry
            - text: .
            - superscript [ref=e636]:
              - link "[30]" [ref=e637] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-41"
            - text: Others, including the black locust (
            - link "Robinia pseudoacacia" [ref=e639] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Robinia_pseudoacacia
            - text: ),
            - superscript [ref=e640]:
              - link "[31]" [ref=e641] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-42"
            - text: Kentucky coffeetree (
            - link "Gymnocladus dioicus" [ref=e643] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Kentucky_coffeetree
            - text: ),
            - superscript [ref=e644]:
              - link "[32]" [ref=e645] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-43"
            - generic [ref=e646]:
              - link "Laburnum" [ref=e647] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: /wiki/Laburnum
              - text: ","
            - superscript [ref=e648]:
              - link "[33]" [ref=e649] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-44"
            - text: and the woody climbing vine
            - link "Wisteria" [ref=e651] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Wisteria
            - text: ", have"
            - link "poisonous" [ref=e652] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Poison
            - text: elements.
          - generic [ref=e653]:
            - heading "History" [level=2] [ref=e654]
            - generic [ref=e655]:

          - paragraph [ref=e657]:
            - link "Neanderthals" [ref=e658] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Neanderthal
            - text: and
            - link "early modern humans" [ref=e659] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Early_modern_humans
            - text: used wild pulses when cooking meals 70,000 to 40,000 years ago.
            - superscript [ref=e660]:
              - link "[34]" [ref=e661] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-45"
            - text: Traces of pulse production have been found around the
            - link "Ravi River" [ref=e662] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Ravi_River
            - text: (
            - link "Punjab" [ref=e663] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Punjab_(region)
            - text: ), the seat of the
            - link "Indus Valley civilisation" [ref=e664] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Indus_Valley_civilisation
            - text: ", from c. 3300 BC. Meanwhile, evidence of lentil cultivation has also been found in Egyptian"
            - link "pyramids" [ref=e665] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Pyramid
            - text: and
            - link "cuneiform" [ref=e666] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Cuneiform
            - link "recipes" [ref=e667] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Recipe
            - text: .
            - superscript [ref=e668]:
              - link "[35]" [ref=e669] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-Albala2007-46"
            - text: Dry pea seeds have been discovered in a Swiss village that are believed to date back to the
            - link "Stone Age" [ref=e670] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Stone_Age
            - text: . Archaeological evidence suggests that these peas must have been grown in the eastern Mediterranean and
            - link "Mesopotamian" [ref=e671] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Mesopotamia
            - text: regions at least 5,000 years ago and in Britain as early as the 11th century.
            - superscript [ref=e672]:
              - link "[36]" [ref=e673] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-b1-47"
            - text: The soybean was domesticated around 5,000 years ago in China from a descendant of the wild vine Glycine soja.
            - superscript [ref=e674]:
              - link "[37]" [ref=e675] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-48"
          - paragraph [ref=e676]:
            - text: The oldest-known domesticated beans in the Americas were found in
            - link "Guitarrero Cave" [ref=e677] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Guitarrero_Cave
            - text: ", an archaeological site in"
            - link "Peru" [ref=e678] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Peru
            - text: ", and dated to around the second millennium BCE."
            - superscript [ref=e679]:
              - link "[38]" [ref=e680] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-Chazan-49"
            - text: Genetic analyses of the common bean Phaseolus show that it originated in
            - link "Mesoamerica" [ref=e681] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Mesoamerica
            - text: ", and subsequently spread southward, along with"
            - link "maize" [ref=e682] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Maize
            - text: and squash, traditional companion crops.
            - superscript [ref=e683]:
              - link "[39]" [ref=e684] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-50"
            - text: In the United States, the domesticated soybean was introduced in 1770 by
            - link "Benjamin Franklin" [ref=e685] [cursor=pointer]:
              - /url: /wiki/Benjamin_Franklin
            - text: after he sent seeds to Philadelphia from France.
            - superscript [ref=e686]:
              - link "[40]" [ref=e687] [cursor=pointer]:
                - /url: "#cite_note-51"

            - link [ref=e695] [cursor=pointer]:
